Worldwide, over 100,000 species of arachnid are known.
Almost all arachnids live on land and are predators.
Ticks and mites are also arachnids.

abschnitte.text: The body of an arachnid consists of two parts: the **front body** with the head, eyes, mouthparts and the eight legs, and the abdomen with the inner organs. At the front sit two jaw claws, which are called chelicerae, and two palps. Arachnids have no antennae like insects. Like all arthropods, they carry a hard armour on the outside and have to moult in order to grow.

The largest group are the **true spiders** with about 50,000 known species. Besides them come scorpions with their venomous sting, harvestmen with a small round body and long legs, and the tiny mites and ticks. Pseudoscorpions, which are only a few millimetres in size, also belong. All of them together form the class of arachnids.

The European garden spider is one of the best-known spiders in Switzerland. On its abdomen it has a pale pattern that looks like a **cross**. In late summer it builds large orb webs in gardens and hedges. Like all arachnids, its body consists of two parts.

Most arachnids are **predators** and eat insects or other small animals. Spiders often catch their prey with webs or lie in wait for it and kill it with venom. Since they cannot chew, they inject digestive juice into the prey and then suck it out. Ticks and some mites, on the other hand, suck blood.

In Switzerland almost 1,000 different species of spider live. None of them is dangerous to healthy people, even though a very few, such as the yellow sac spider, can bite painfully. More important are the **ticks**, which can transmit diseases such as tick-borne encephalitis and Lyme disease. After a walk in the forest, you should therefore check your body for ticks.

begriffe.erklaerung: Jaw claws at the front of the head of arachnids, with venom glands in spiders.
The front part of the body with the head, eyes and legs.
The rear part of the body with the digestion, the heart and, in spiders, the spinnerets.
A huge group of animals with an outer armour and jointed legs, including insects and arachnids.

gewusst: Worldwide, spiders are estimated to eat several hundred million tonnes of insects every year.
Harvestmen are not spiders and have neither venom glands nor spinnerets.
Scorpions glow blue green under ultraviolet light.

teile.einleitung: The Tatra chamois is a rare subspecies of the chamois that lives only in the High Tatras, a high mountain range on the border between Slovakia and Poland. It is closely related to the chamois in the Swiss Alps. Because at times there were only a few hundred animals left, it is strictly protected.
wichtigste: The Tatra chamois (Rupicapra rupicapra tatrica) is a subspecies of the chamois.
It lives only in the Tatras in Slovakia and Poland.
Around the year 2000 there were only a few hundred animals left.
Thanks to strict protection, the population has grown again to over a thousand animals.
It is a symbol of the Tatra national parks.
Like all chamois, it climbs surely on steep rock.

abschnitte.text: The **Tatras** are the highest mountain range of the Carpathians, and their highest peak is Gerlachovský štít at about 2655 metres. Here the Tatra chamois lives on rock faces, scree slopes and alpine meadows above the tree line. In winter it often comes down a little lower, where it finds food more easily. Outside the Tatras this **subspecies** is not found naturally anywhere.

The Tatra chamois looks very much like the Alpine chamois. Both sexes have short, black, hook-shaped **horns** that curve backwards, which in German are called Krucken. In summer the coat is reddish brown, and in winter it is dense and almost black. Typical is the light face with a dark stripe from the horn over the eye to the mouth.

Chamois eat grasses, herbs, lichens, buds and in winter also needles and shoots. The females live with the young in **herds**, older bucks often alone. In late autumn is the mating season, which is called the **rut**. In early summer a single young one is usually born, which can climb after only a few hours.

Through hunting, poaching and disturbance by tourism, the population shrank sharply. Around the year 2000 only a few hundred animals lived in the Tatras. The **national parks** on the Slovak and Polish sides protect the animals together and count them every year. By now clearly over a thousand Tatra chamois live in the mountains again, and the animal appears in the logo of the Polish Tatra National Park.

In the Swiss Alps and in the Jura lives the **Alpine chamois**, the most common subspecies. There are about 90 000 chamois in Switzerland. Here they are popular game, and the long tuft of back hair of the bucks is worn on hats as a **Gamsbart**, a chamois beard. The Tatra chamois, on the other hand, is so rare that it may not be hunted at all.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group within an animal species that lives in a particular area and differs a little.
The hook-shaped horns of the chamois.
The mating season in deer, chamois and other hoofed animals.
A large protected area in which nature is allowed to develop as undisturbed as possible.

gewusst: Chamois can stand on almost vertical rock faces because their hooves have hard edges and a soft, grippy sole.
The High Tatras are much smaller than the Alps, but are regarded as the smallest high mountain range in the world with a truly alpine character.
The Slovak Tatra National Park was founded in 1949 and is the oldest national park in Slovakia.

teile.einleitung: Rabies is a dangerous viral disease that attacks the brain and can be passed on from animals to people. In Switzerland dogs are vaccinated against rabies regularly. Thanks to vaccinations, Switzerland is regarded today as free of rabies in land animals.
wichtigste: Rabies is a viral disease that attacks the nervous system.
It is mostly passed on through bites and the saliva of infected animals.
Dogs are vaccinated regularly against rabies in Switzerland.
Once the disease breaks out, it almost always ends in death.
A vaccination soon after a bite can prevent the disease from breaking out.
Louis Pasteur developed the first rabies vaccine for people in 1885.
Switzerland defeated fox rabies with vaccine baits.

abschnitte.text: Rabies is caused by a **virus** that belongs to the lyssaviruses. The virus travels along the nerves to the brain. Sick animals often become restless, aggressive or lose their fear of people, while others become dull and paralysed. The German word for rabies, Tollwut, uses “toll”, which used to mean “mad”.

Rabies is passed on mainly through **bites**, because the virus is in the saliva. Worldwide, dogs are the most important source of infection for people. In Europe it used to be mainly foxes that played a big part. Bats can also carry rabies viruses, which is why you should never touch sick or injured bats with bare hands.

There is an effective **vaccination** against rabies for animals and people. The first vaccine for people was used by Louis Pasteur in 1885 on nine-year-old Joseph Meister, who had been bitten by a rabid dog. If someone is bitten, they must go to a doctor at once, because a quick vaccination prevents the disease from breaking out. Dogs and cats that travel abroad need a valid rabies vaccination.

In 1967 fox rabies reached Switzerland from Germany. In 1978 researchers in the Valais laid out **vaccine baits** for foxes for the first time anywhere in the world, that is, chicken heads containing vaccine. This method was so successful that it was later taken up all over Europe. Since 1999 Switzerland has been regarded as free of rabies in land animals, although the virus still very rarely occurs in bats.

Worldwide an estimated 59 000 people or so die of rabies every year, mainly in Asia and Africa. Many of them are children who were bitten by dogs. The World Health Organization wants to make sure that nobody dies of rabies from dogs any more. **World Rabies Day** on 28 September reminds people of this disease every year.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny germ that causes disease and can multiply only inside living cells.
A lump of food containing vaccine that wild animals eat and are protected by.
The fluid in the mouth, also called spit.
A substance that teaches the body to fight off a disease.

gewusst: Switzerland was the first country in the world to vaccinate foxes against rabies with vaccine baits.
An old German word for rabies is “Hundswut”, meaning dog madness.
Because people with rabies often get spasms when swallowing, they used to be said to have a “fear of water”.

teile.einleitung: The Svalbard reindeer is a small subspecies of the reindeer that lives only on the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard. It is smaller and shorter legged than its relatives on the mainland. So it is perfectly adapted to cold, wind and the long polar night.
wichtigste: The Svalbard reindeer lives only on Svalbard in the Arctic Ocean.
It is small and short legged and has a roundish body.
Its dense fur and a thick layer of fat protect it from the cold.
It lives alone or in small groups and hardly migrates far.
In winter it scrapes the snow away to get at lichens and plants.
After heavy hunting it was put under protection in 1925.
Today about 20,000 of these reindeer live on Svalbard again (estimate around 2020).

abschnitte.text: The Svalbard reindeer is the smallest form of the **reindeer**. It has short legs, a short head and small ears, which means it loses less heat. In autumn, thanks to its fat reserves, it is quite roundish, whereas in late winter it is clearly lighter. As in all reindeer, both males and females carry antlers.

**Svalbard** lies far in the north between Norway and the North Pole. There, in winter, darkness and icy temperatures prevail for months, and in summer the sun shines day and night. The reindeer live on the snow-free areas of the valleys and coasts. Because there are no wolves on the archipelago, they hardly have to flee from predators.

In the short Arctic summer the animals eat grasses, mosses, herbs and dwarf shrubs, and in doing so build up a thick **layer of fat**. In winter they scrape the snow away with their hooves to get at lichens and plant remains. It becomes dangerous when rain falls on snow and freezes. Then the food lies under a hard layer of ice, and many animals can starve.

Unlike the large reindeer herds in Scandinavia, Svalbard reindeer mostly live alone or in **small groups**. They do not migrate long distances, but stay in their area. In winter they move little in order to save energy. The calves are born in early summer.

In the past, the reindeer on Svalbard were hunted so heavily by hunters and trappers that they almost disappeared. Since **1925** they have been protected, and the population has recovered well. Today experts study how **climate change** affects the animals. Milder winters with more rain make life harder for them, while longer summers bring more food.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group within an animal species that differs somewhat from the others.
A time in winter when the sun does not rise at all in the Arctic.
A partnership of a fungus and an alga, an important winter food for reindeer.
A bony outgrowth on the head that is shed every year and grows back.

gewusst: Reindeer are the only deer in which the females also carry antlers.
In autumn a Svalbard reindeer can carry a large part of its weight as fat.
Because there are no wolves on Svalbard, the polar bear is practically the only enemy that can become dangerous to an adult reindeer.

teile.einleitung: Myriapods, in German called Tausendfüsser or “thousand-footers”, are arthropods with a long body of many similar rings, on which many legs sit. They include the nimble centipedes and the slow-moving millipedes, which you find under leaves, stones and wood. By the way, not a single species has exactly a thousand legs.
wichtigste: Myriapods belong to the arthropods, like insects, spiders and crustaceans.
The group is called Myriapoda in science and includes centipedes, millipedes, pauropods and symphylans.
Their body consists of many similar trunk segments with legs.
No myriapod has exactly a thousand legs, and most have far fewer.
In central Europe they mostly live in the soil, under leaves, stones and wood.
They need moisture and are mostly active at night, because otherwise they dry out easily.
Myriapods have existed for about 420 million years, and they are among the first land animals.

abschnitte.text: Myriapods or **Myriapoda** are a group of **arthropods** with over 15 000 known species worldwide. Their body consists of a head and a long trunk made up of many identically built sections, the **segments**. Unlike insects, they therefore do not have a trunk made of a chest and an abdomen with only six legs. On the head they have a pair of antennae, with which they mainly feel and smell.

The **centipedes** have one pair of legs per segment and are fast predators with venom claws on the head. The **millipedes** have two pairs of legs on most segments and eat mainly rotting plants. Added to these are the tiny, soft **pauropods** and **symphylans**, which grow to only a few millimetres. The number of legs ranges, depending on the species, from about 20 to over 1000.

In central Europe, myriapods live in the soil, under leaves, stones, bark and dead wood. Their skin has no waterproof layer of wax as insects have, so they **dry out easily**. That is why most are out and about at night, when it is cooler and damper. Some species have simple eyes, but many are blind and find their way with their antennae.

Millipedes break up fallen leaves and dead wood and so help to form fertile **humus**. Centipedes hunt insects, spiders and worms and keep their numbers in check. To defend themselves, some millipedes such as the pill millipede roll up into a ball. Others give off foul-smelling or caustic fluids to scare off enemies.

In Swiss gardens and woods you often find the brown **stone centipede**, a nimble centipede. Under leaves live flat-backed and snake millipedes that coil up in a spiral when disturbed, and the rolling pill millipedes. In Ticino, and increasingly also north of the Alps, the long-legged **house centipede** is found in houses. The native species are harmless to people.

Myriapods have existed for about 420 million years, which makes them among the oldest known land animals. A fossil millipede from Scotland is one of the earliest animals that breathed air. In the Carboniferous, about 300 million years ago, lived the giant myriapod **Arthropleura**, which could grow over two metres long. It is the largest known arthropod that ever lived on land.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals with a hard outer skeleton and jointed legs, such as insects, spiders, crustaceans and myriapods.
One of the many similar sections that make up the body.
The scientific name of the myriapods, meaning “countless feet”.
Dark, fertile soil made of decomposed plant remains.

gewusst: Only in 2021 was a myriapod discovered in Australia, Eumillipes persephone, that really has over a thousand legs, namely up to 1306.
Young millipedes hatch with only a few pairs of legs and get new segments and legs with every moult.
Some tropical centipedes grow over 25 centimetres long and even catch mice and bats.

teile.einleitung: In textile technology, spinning is the process by which a thread is made from loose fibres. Before you can knit or weave anything, the wool must first be spun. From the simple wooden stick to the huge spinning machine, this technique has a long history.
wichtigste: Spinning means twisting fibres into a thread before you knit or weave something from it.
The oldest tool for spinning is the hand spindle.
The spinning wheel came to Europe in the Middle Ages and made the work faster.
In the 18th century the first spinning machines were invented in England.
Spinning machines were a starting point of the Industrial Revolution.
Today machines also spin man-made fibres such as polyester.
A factory in which spinning is done is called a spinning mill.

abschnitte.text: The **hand spindle** is a wooden stick with a small disc as a weight to give it swing. You spin it like a top, and the twist travels into the fibres and makes a thread of them. As early as the Stone Age, people spun wool and plant fibres in this way. Finds of spindle whorls, the weights, also exist from pile dwellings in Switzerland.

The **spinning wheel** is driven by hand or with a foot pedal. A large wheel makes the bobbin turn quickly by means of a cord. In this way one person can spin clearly more and more even thread than with the hand spindle. In fairy tales such as Sleeping Beauty or Rumpelstiltskin, the spinning wheel plays an important role.

In 1764 James Hargreaves in England invented the **spinning jenny**, which could spin several threads at the same time. Soon still bigger machines followed, which ran on water power and later on steam engines. Suddenly factories could make a very great deal of yarn cheaply. Many people who had spun at home lost their work as a result.

In Switzerland, from the beginning of the 19th century, many **spinning mills** arose, for example in the Zurich Oberland and in eastern Switzerland. They mostly stood on rivers, because water wheels drove the machines. Many children also worked in the factories, until laws restricted child labour. Today, for instance, the Zurich Oberland industrial trail still shows old spinning mill buildings.

Modern spinning machines turn thousands of spindles at the same time at very high speed. Besides wool and cotton, **man-made fibres** such as polyester and nylon are also processed, which are made from crude oil. Man-made fibres come about when liquid plastic is pressed through fine nozzles. But many people still spin by hand today as a hobby.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rotating stick on which the spun thread is wound.
A small weight on the hand spindle that gives it swing.
A factory in which fibres are spun into yarn.
A fibre that does not come from an animal or plant, but is made artificially.

gewusst: The spinning jenny is said to be named after the daughter or wife of the inventor, but that is not certain.
The German word spinnen is also used for the spinning of spiders, because they too make threads.
In the fairy tale Rumpelstiltskin, straw is supposed to be spun into gold.

teile.einleitung: The Animal Welfare Act is a federal law that sets out in Switzerland how people have to treat animals. It protects the dignity and well-being of animals. Among other things, it also regulates the duty to mark dogs with a microchip.
wichtigste: The Animal Welfare Act protects the dignity and well-being of animals.
The current law dates from 2005 and has been in force since 1 September 2008.
More detailed rules are set out in the Animal Welfare Ordinance.
Among other things, the law regulates the duty to mark dogs with a microchip.
Social animals such as guinea pigs may not be kept alone.
The cantonal veterinary offices are responsible for checks.
Since 2003 animals are no longer regarded as things in Swiss law.

abschnitte.text: The Animal Welfare Act, TSchG for short in German, is a law of the Confederation. It applies to all vertebrates and to some invertebrates such as octopuses and decapod crustaceans. The aim is to protect the **dignity** and well-being of animals. Nobody may cause an animal pain, suffering or fear without reason.

The first federal animal welfare law came into force in 1978. The current law was passed on 16 December 2005 and came into force on 1 September 2008. As early as 1992, Switzerland wrote the “dignity of creatures” into its Federal Constitution, as one of the first countries in the world. Exact rules, for example how big an enclosure has to be, are set out in the **Animal Welfare Ordinance**.

Anyone who keeps an animal has to feed it properly, care for it and give it enough space and things to do. Social animals such as guinea pigs, rabbits or budgerigars may not be kept alone. Dogs have to be marked with a **microchip** and registered in the Amicus database. Docking, that is, cutting off the ears or tail of dogs, is forbidden.

Cows, pigs and hens are protected as well, for example through minimum sizes for stables and rules for transport. Many Swiss rules go further than those of neighbouring countries. **Animal experiments** are allowed only with a permit and have to be well justified. A commission checks whether the benefit is greater than the suffering of the animals.

The **cantonal veterinary offices** are responsible for checks. Anyone who tortures or neglects animals can be punished, in serious cases even with prison. The authorities can take animals away from a keeper and forbid them to keep animals. Anyone who sees cruelty to animals can report it to the veterinary office.

begriffe.erklaerung: The idea that animals have a value of their own and must be treated with respect.
A supplement to a law with exact details.
A cantonal authority for animal welfare and animal health.
A chip the size of a grain of rice under the skin with a number that can be used to find the keeper.

gewusst: Anyone who kept a dog in Switzerland was required between 2008 and 2016 to attend a dog course.
Since 2003 the Swiss Civil Code has included the sentence that animals are not things.
Since 2018, lobsters may also no longer be thrown alive into boiling water in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A closed season is a fixed time of year in which certain animals may not be hunted or fished. It protects the animals above all during reproduction and the raising of the young. In Switzerland it is regulated in the hunting and fishing laws and in the laws of the cantons.
wichtigste: During the closed season, certain animals may not be hunted or caught.
It protects the animals above all in the time of reproduction and raising the young.
Fishes such as lake trout and whitefish have closed seasons so that they can reproduce undisturbed.
In Switzerland, the federal hunting law and fishing law regulate the closed seasons.
The cantons may lengthen the closed seasons, but not shorten them.
Many fishes also have a minimum size limit.
Anyone who hunts or fishes in the closed season commits an offence.

abschnitte.text: A **closed season** is a period in which a species of animal may not be hunted, caught or fished. The opposite is called the **open season** or fishing season. There are closed seasons for wild animals such as roe deer, red deer, chamois and birds, and for many fishes. They mostly fall in the time when the animals mate, spawn or raise their young. In this way the population can recover every year.

Fishes are especially sensitive when they **spawn**, that is, lay their eggs. The lake trout migrates for this in autumn from the lakes into rivers and streams. Whitefish spawn in late autumn and winter in the lakes. During this time they are protected so that they can reproduce undisturbed. In addition, many fishes have a **minimum size limit**: a fish that is too small must be released again.

In hunting, the federal **hunting law** lays down closed seasons. The chamois, for example, is protected from 1 January to 31 July. In this time the young are born and suckled. Mothers that are still leading young are especially protected. Many species of animals such as the lynx, the beaver or most birds of prey may never be hunted at all.

In Switzerland, the **Confederation** sets the basic rules in the hunting law and the fishing law. The **cantons** put them into practice and fix the exact dates. They may lengthen closed seasons, but not shorten them. That is why the dates can be somewhat different depending on the canton and the lake. Anyone who wants to fish needs a licence, called a Patent in Switzerland, and must know the rules of their canton.

Without closed seasons, animals could be hunted or fished so heavily that their populations collapse. With closed seasons, only as much is used as can grow back. This is called **sustainability**. In this way wild animals and fishes are preserved for future generations too. For hikers, too, there are wildlife quiet zones in winter, so that the animals are not disturbed.

begriffe.erklaerung: The laying of eggs by fishes and amphibians.
The minimum size a fish must have for it to be kept.
A permit, for example for fishing or hunting, called a Patent in Switzerland.
Using only as much as can grow back.

gewusst: As early as the Middle Ages there were rules about when certain animals might not be hunted.
In the closed season, some fishes are caught by fishery wardens in order to raise their eggs in fish hatcheries.

teile.einleitung: Butterflies are insects with four often brightly patterned wings that lived earlier as caterpillars. Their transformation from caterpillar through pupa to butterfly is one of the great wonders of nature. They drink nectar and in doing so pollinate many flowers.
wichtigste: Butterflies are insects with six legs and four wings.
Their body consists of head, thorax and abdomen.
A caterpillar hatches from the egg, pupates and becomes a butterfly.
The wings are covered with tiny scales and crossed by wing veins.
With their feet, butterflies taste whether a flower is sweet.
Butterflies have no sting and flee when in danger.
In Switzerland live over 3,000 species of butterflies and moths, most of them moths.

abschnitte.text: Like all insects, butterflies have six legs and a body in three parts: head, thorax and abdomen. On the thorax sit **four wings**, two forewings and two hindwings. The wings are covered with tiny **scales** that lie on top of one another like roof tiles and form the colours. Pale lines like a net, the wing veins, support the wings. For drinking, butterflies have a long **proboscis**, which they can roll up.

A female butterfly lays her eggs on particular food plants. From the egg hatches a **caterpillar**, which eats a lot and moults several times. Then it pupates, and inside the **pupa** the body is completely rebuilt. This transformation is called complete **metamorphosis**. The freshly hatched butterfly must first pump up its soft, crumpled wings and let them dry.

Adult butterflies drink mainly **nectar** from flowers, and some also drink juice from rotting fruit. In doing so they carry pollen from flower to flower and so help with pollination. On their feet they have sense cells with which they can taste whether something is sweet. The caterpillars, by contrast, eat leaves, often only from quite particular plants. The caterpillar of the peacock butterfly, for example, eats mainly stinging nettles.

Butterflies are cold-blooded and need warmth in order to fly. If it is too cold, they stay put, and on cool mornings they warm themselves in the sun with their wings spread. When in danger they mostly fly away quickly, because they have no sting like a bee. Some frighten enemies with **eyespots** on the wings. People distinguish butterflies that fly by day and the far more numerous moths.

In Switzerland live over 3,000 species of butterflies and moths, of which about 200 are day-flying butterflies. Well-known species are the brimstone, the peacock, the small tortoiseshell, the swallowtail and the Apollo in the Alps. The brimstone spends the winter as an adult butterfly and is often one of the first in spring. Many species are endangered and are on the **Red List**.

Butterflies need wildflower meadows for food and for laying eggs. Because many meadows are fertilised, mown often or built over, their habitats are disappearing. Plant protection products also harm them. Everyone can help: with a **wildflower corner** in the garden, native plants and a few stinging nettles that are allowed to stay.

begriffe.erklaerung: The transformation from caterpillar through pupa to butterfly.
The larva of a butterfly.
A long, rollable sucking tube for drinking nectar.
The transfer of pollen so that plants can form seeds.

gewusst: The monarch butterfly travels thousands of kilometres every year from Canada to Mexico.
The painted lady flies every spring from North Africa over the Alps into Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Silk Road was a huge network of trade routes between China and the Mediterranean. Caravans with Bactrian camels travelled across deserts and mountains and brought silk, spices and new ideas from one end of the world to the other.
wichtigste: For many centuries the Silk Road connected China with Central Asia, Persia and the Mediterranean region.
It was not a single road, but a network of many routes.
The name was coined in 1877 by the German researcher Ferdinand von Richthofen.
Caravans used mainly Bactrian camels, which cope well with heat and cold.
Silk, porcelain, spices, glass, horses and much more were traded.
Religions, inventions and, unfortunately, diseases too spread along these routes.

abschnitte.text: The Silk Road was a network of **trade routes** over land that connected East Asia with Europe and North Africa. It began in the old Chinese capital Chang'an, today's Xi'an. From there the routes led through deserts and over mountains to ports on the Mediterranean. In all that was several thousand kilometres. Hardly any merchant travelled the whole distance, and the goods changed hands many times on the way.

The most important animal of the Silk Road was the **Bactrian camel**, a camel with two humps. It can manage for days without water and endures both glowing heat and icy winters. Its thick winter coat protects it in the cold deserts of Central Asia such as the Gobi. A Bactrian camel can carry heavy loads over long distances. Many animals one behind the other formed a **caravan**.

From about the 2nd century BC, the Silk Road was heavily used under the Chinese Han dynasty. It flourished over many centuries into the Middle Ages. In the 13th century the Venetian **Marco Polo** travelled along these routes as far as China. Later, trade by ship across the sea became more important, and the land routes lost significance.

From China came above all **silk**, a precious cloth whose manufacture was long a secret. Porcelain, tea, paper and spices were also traded. In the other direction went gold, silver, glass, wool and horses. Religions such as Buddhism also spread along the Silk Road. Unfortunately diseases travelled with it too, probably the plague as well.

Along the routes there were **caravanserais**, which were rest houses with a courtyard in which people and animals could spend the night. Famous oasis cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara in Uzbekistan grew rich through the trade. Today parts of the Silk Road are UNESCO World Heritage. China uses the name “New Silk Road” for modern rail, road and port projects.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of merchants who travel together with pack animals.
A camel with two humps from Central Asia.
A rest house for caravans with room for people, animals and goods.
A place with water and plants in the middle of the desert.

gewusst: The silkworm, from whose cocoon silk is obtained, was for a long time a closely guarded secret in China.
The name “Silk Road” is much younger than the trade routes themselves, and dates only from 1877.
A Bactrian camel can drink over 100 litres of water at one go.

teile.einleitung: The Toggenburg goat is a Swiss breed of goat from the Toggenburg in the canton of St Gallen. You can recognise it by its brown coat with white stripes on the face. It is a good dairy goat and is kept all over the world today.
wichtigste: The Toggenburg goat comes from the Toggenburg in the canton of St Gallen.
Its coat is mostly brown with white stripes on the face.
It is a dairy goat.
Most Toggenburg goats have no horns.
The breed has been exported to many countries, for example to England and the USA.
Switzerland has many breeds of goat of its own.

abschnitte.text: The coat of the Toggenburg goat is mostly light brown to mouse grey. Typical are two **white stripes** on the face, running from the eyes to the muzzle. The ears are also edged in white, and the lower legs and the area around the tail are white. Most animals are **hornless**, and some have small flaps of skin on the neck that are called wattles.

The breed comes from the **Toggenburg**, the valley of the upper Thur between the Säntis and the Churfirsten in the canton of St Gallen. There farming families have kept goats for milk and meat for a long time. In the 19th century the breed was bred on purpose and recorded in a herd book. The aim was a hardy goat that gives plenty of milk even in the harsh mountain climate.

The Toggenburg goat is an excellent **dairy goat**. A nanny gives several hundred litres of milk a year. Cheese, yoghurt and butter are made from goat's milk, and it tastes a little stronger than cow's milk. Because the goat is hardy and calm, it is also well suited to small farms and hobby keepers.

From the late 19th century, Toggenburg goats were taken to Great Britain, the USA and many other countries. There, lines of their own were developed, such as the British Toggenburg. In America the Toggenburg is among the best-known dairy goats. In Switzerland itself the breed is now rarer than the white **Saanen goat**.

Switzerland has a surprising number of breeds of goat of its own. They include the Saanen goat, the Chamois Coloured goat, the Appenzell goat, the Grisons Striped goat, the Valais Blackneck goat and the Peacock goat. Some of these breeds are rare and are supported by the foundation **Pro Specie Rara**. Goats are ruminants and good climbers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of domestic animals with the same typical features.
The Swiss word for a female goat, and its young is called a Gitzi.
A breeding book in which the ancestry and performance of the animals are recorded.
An animal that brings its food back up and chews it a second time.

gewusst: Goats are among the oldest domestic animals and were tamed in the Near East as long ago as about 10 000 years.
The male goat is called a buck and smells very strong in the breeding season.
Goats can even climb sloping trees to reach leaves.

teile.einleitung: The stag beetles, in German Schröter, are a family of beetles that includes the famous European stag beetle. In many males the mandibles are huge and look like antlers. Their larvae grow up for years in rotting wood.
wichtigste: The stag beetles are a family of beetles with the scientific name Lucanidae.
Worldwide there are over a thousand species, most of them in warm countries.
The European stag beetle is the best known stag beetle and the largest beetle in central Europe.
Many males have greatly enlarged upper jaws, which are called mandibles.
The larvae eat dead, rotting wood and need several years for their development.
In Switzerland live, among others, the European stag beetle, the lesser stag beetle and the rhinoceros stag beetle.
Because old trees and dead wood are lacking, some stag beetles have become rare.

abschnitte.text: Stag beetles have a firm body, mostly brown to black. Typical are the **antennae**, which look elbowed, with a comb-like tip. In the males of many species the **mandibles**, that is, the upper jaws, are especially large. In the European stag beetle they are reminiscent of a stag's antlers, hence the name.

Stag beetles live mainly in forests, parks and old orchards. **Dead wood** is important for them, that is, dead trunks, stumps and roots. The European stag beetle especially likes old oaks in warm places. The lesser stag beetle is more common and also lives in beech and mixed forests.

The female lays her eggs in the soil next to rotting wood or directly into it. The white, curved **larvae** gnaw their way through the wood for years. In the European stag beetle this often takes five years or even longer. Afterwards they pupate and hatch as a finished beetle that lives only a few weeks.

In early summer, male stag beetles fight over the females. They grab each other with their **antlers** and try to throw the opponent off the branch. They are rarely injured in doing so. The adult beetles feed on **tree sap**, which flows from wounds in the bark.

The European stag beetle is protected throughout Europe and is also regarded as rare and worth protecting in Switzerland. You find it mainly in lower, warm regions, for example in Ticino, in Valais and along the southern foot of the Jura. For stag beetles to survive, **dead wood** is left lying in forests and old oaks are left standing. Some conservationists even build stag beetle piles from logs in which larvae can develop.

begriffe.erklaerung: The upper jaws of an insect, with which it bites or grips.
Dead wood from trees that slowly rots.
The young stage of an insect, which looks quite different from the adult animal.
A group of closely related animal species.

gewusst: Male stag beetles can grow up to about 8 centimetres long, including the antlers.
The German name Schröter comes from the old word schroten, which means to cut up.

teile.einleitung: Sheep's wool is the coat of the sheep, from which people have made warm clothes for thousands of years. A sheep's whole woolly coat is called a fleece. Wool keeps you warm, takes up moisture and burns poorly, which makes it a special natural material.
wichtigste: A sheep's whole woolly coat is called a fleece.
Wool can be white, black, brown or mixed.
Sheep's wool is made into warm jumpers, socks, hats and blankets.
A lamb often has especially soft, curly wool before its first shearing.
Wool consists of keratin, the same protein as our hair.
The wool grease lanolin makes the wool water repellent.
The Merino sheep gives especially fine wool.

abschnitte.text: Wool is the fine, crimped **hair** of the sheep. It consists of the protein **keratin**, like our hair and fingernails. The whole woolly coat is called a fleece. The colour can be white, black, brown or mixed, and white wool is the most common, because it can be dyed easily.

Wool fibres are wavy, and a lot of air stays trapped between them, which **insulates** well. Wool can take up a lot of moisture and still does not feel wet. It burns poorly and hardly takes on smells. The wool grease **lanolin** keeps out rain and is also used in ointments and creams.

After shearing, the wool is washed to remove dirt and grease. Then it is combed so that the fibres lie in one direction. In **spinning**, the fibres are twisted into a yarn. From the yarn you can knit, weave or crochet, and with water, soap and rubbing, felt is made.

The finest wool comes from the **Merino sheep**, whose fibres are very thin and soft. Coarser wool is suitable for carpets or insulation. Lamb's wool from the first shearing is especially soft, because the tips of the hairs are still fine. Large wool producers are Australia, China and New Zealand.

In Switzerland live about 350,000 sheep, for example the White Alpine sheep and the Black-Brown Mountain sheep (as of around 2024). Most of them, however, are kept for meat and landscape care, not for the wool. Swiss wool is partly collected and made into bedding, **insulation** or yarn. Many wool products in shops, however, come from abroad.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sheep's whole woolly coat.
A firm protein of which hair, nails and wool consist.
Grease from sheep's wool that repels water.
The twisting of fibres into a thread.

gewusst: A woollen jumper can take up to about a third of its weight in water without feeling wet.
Wool is one of the oldest materials for clothes, and people have used it for several thousand years.

teile.einleitung: The seven-spot ladybird is the best-known ladybird in Switzerland. With its red wing cases and seven black spots, it counts as a good luck charm. For gardeners it is a valuable helper, because it eats masses of aphids.
wichtigste: The seven-spot ladybird has seven black spots on red wing cases.
It is about 5 to 8 millimetres in size.
The beetles and larvae eat mainly aphids.
That is why it is a beneficial insect in the garden and in agriculture.
It spends the winter as an adult beetle, often in groups.
When in danger, it gives off a yellow, bitter fluid.
Its spots do not reveal its age.

abschnitte.text: The seven-spot ladybird is rounded and about 5 to 8 millimetres in size. Its hard red **wing cases** carry seven black spots: three on each side and one at the front in the middle that extends across both sides. Underneath, the delicate wings are folded for flying. The head and the pronotum are black with white patches. The bright colours warn birds: I taste bad!

You find it in gardens, on meadows, fields, at the edges of forests and in parks. It is widespread throughout Europe and in large parts of Asia and North Africa. In Switzerland it occurs from the lowlands up high into the mountains. It is wherever there are many **aphids**.

Both the beetle and its **larva** eat mainly aphids. A larva eats several hundred aphids during its development. An adult beetle can eat several thousand in the course of its life. That is why it is a popular **beneficial insect** that helps to protect plants without poison.

In spring the female lays small yellow eggs in groups on plants, often near an aphid colony. From them hatch dark, elongated larvae with small warts that do not look like a ladybird at all. After some weeks they pupate, and the finished beetle hatches from the **pupa**. At first it is still pale yellow, and only after hours does it turn red.

In autumn the beetles look for sheltered places, for example under leaves, bark or in cracks in walls. There they often spend the winter close together in **groups**. When in danger they play dead and give off a yellow, bitter fluid at the leg joints, which is called **reflex bleeding**. In recent years the introduced harlequin ladybird has been competing with it.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hard forewings of a beetle that protect the hindwings.
The young form of an insect that looks different from the adult animal.
An animal that helps people, for example by eating pests.
Giving off a bad-tasting fluid to ward off enemies.

gewusst: The number of spots does not show a ladybird's age, but depends on the species.
The German name Marienkäfer, meaning Mary's beetle, recalls Mary, the mother of Jesus, because the beetle was seen as a gift from heaven.
Freshly hatched seven-spot ladybirds are at first pale yellow and have no spots yet.

teile.einleitung: The Bactrian camel is a camel with two humps that lives in the cold deserts and steppes of Central Asia. It can stand scorching heat in summer and icy cold in winter. For thousands of years Bactrian camels have carried loads through the Gobi Desert.
wichtigste: The Bactrian camel has two humps.
It is a mammal and belongs to the camel family.
The humps store mainly fat, not water.
Wild Bactrian camels now live only in desert areas of Mongolia and China.
Broad feet with calloused soles stop it from sinking into the sand.
In a sandstorm it can close its nostrils.
A female usually gives birth to a single young one.

abschnitte.text: The Bactrian camel is a large **mammal** with two humps on its back. The shoulder height is about 1.80 to 2.30 metres, and fully grown animals weigh several hundred kilograms. The feet are broad and have **calloused soles**, so that the animal does not sink into the sand. Long eyelashes protect the eyes, and in a sandstorm it can close its nostrils.

Bactrian camels live in Central Asia, where the summers are hot and the winters bitterly cold. Their name in many languages recalls the old region of **Bactria**, which lay in the area of present-day Afghanistan. Wild Bactrian camels now live only in desert areas of Mongolia and China, mainly in the Gobi Desert. These wild camels are regarded today as a separate species and are critically endangered.

Bactrian camels eat grasses, shrubs and even thorny or salty plants that other animals avoid. The humps store mainly **fat**, not water. When the animal goes hungry for a long time, the humps become floppy and tip to the side. If it has the chance to drink, a thirsty camel can take in over a hundred litres of water in a few minutes.

In winter the Bactrian camel wears a thick, long coat that protects it from temperatures far below zero. In spring it loses the thick **winter coat** in large tufts. People collect this wool and make warm blankets and clothes from it. In summer the animal therefore often looks a little scruffy.

The mating season of Bactrian camels is in winter. After a gestation of about 13 months, the female usually gives birth to a single young one. The foal can walk just a few hours after birth. It drinks its mother's milk for over a year.

The domestic camel was tamed several thousand years ago and was an important pack animal on the **Silk Road**. As a pack animal it can carry from several dozen up to about 200 kilograms. People in Mongolia still use Bactrian camels today for milk, meat, wool and as animals to ride. By contrast, the dromedary from Arabia and North Africa has only one hump.

begriffe.erklaerung: A raised part on the back of the camel in which fat is stored.
A thick, soft pad of hard skin on the underside of the foot.
The one-humped camel from Arabia and North Africa.
A very old network of trade routes between China and Europe.

gewusst: The red blood cells of camels are oval and not round as in other mammals.
Bactrian camels can stand temperatures of about minus 40 to plus 40 degrees Celsius.
Memory aid: the Bactrian camel has two humps like the letter B for Bactria, and the dromedary has one like the letter D.

teile.einleitung: The swallowtail is a large, yellow and black butterfly that flies by day, with two small points on the hindwings. These points are reminiscent of the forked tail of a swallow. In Switzerland it is often described as the largest native butterfly.
wichtigste: The swallowtail belongs to the swallowtail family and is called Papilio machaon scientifically.
Its wings are yellow with black veins, a blue band and a red eyespot.
Its caterpillar especially likes to eat wild carrot and fennel.
Dill, carrots and other umbellifers are also among its food plants.
When in danger, the caterpillar pushes out an orange neck fork that smells strongly.
The butterfly spends the winter as a pupa.
In Switzerland it occurs from the lowlands high up into the Alps.

abschnitte.text: The **swallowtail** has a wingspan of about 6 to 8 centimetres. Its wings are bright yellow with black veins and black edges. On the hindwing sit a blue band, a red **eyespot** and the typical tail-like extensions. The eyespot and the little tails draw birds away from the butterfly's head.

The caterpillar is at first black with a white patch and looks like bird droppings. Later it becomes green with black cross bands and orange dots. If it is disturbed, it pushes out an orange **neck fork** behind the head. This gives off an unpleasant smell that scares off enemies such as ants.

The caterpillars eat **umbellifers**, especially wild carrot and fennel. Dill, caraway and garden carrots are also accepted. That is why you sometimes find the caterpillars in the vegetable garden. The adult butterflies, by contrast, drink nectar from flowers such as thistles, clover and knapweeds.

In the lowlands there are usually two **generations** a year, the first flying in spring and the second in high summer. In higher places there is often time for only one generation. The caterpillars change into a **girdled pupa**, which hangs from a stem on a silk thread. In this form the swallowtail spends the winter.

Males like to meet on hilltops and mountain summits in order to find females there. This behaviour is called **hilltopping**. In Switzerland the swallowtail is widespread and occurs up to over 2,000 metres. It benefits from flower-rich meadows, verges and natural gardens with fennel or dill.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of large, often colourful butterflies.
Plants whose flowers are arranged like an umbrella, for example carrot and fennel.
A protrusible, smelly organ of the caterpillar for defence.
A pupa that is fastened to a stem with a silk girdle.

gewusst: The young caterpillars disguise themselves as bird droppings so that they are not eaten.
With some fennel or dill in the garden you can attract swallowtails.

teile.einleitung: The housefly is the fly that buzzes through kitchens and living rooms in summer. It is found almost everywhere that people live, and in warm weather it multiplies at lightning speed. It does not bite, but it can pass on disease germs.
wichtigste: The housefly is called Musca domestica in science.
It is found almost everywhere in the world where people live.
Its buzzing comes from its fast wingbeat.
With its compound eyes it spots movement very quickly.
A white larva, the maggot, hatches from the egg.
In warm weather it develops so quickly that there are several generations in one summer.
The housefly does not bite and does not drink blood.

abschnitte.text: The housefly is about 6 to 7 millimetres long. Its chest is grey with four dark stripes along its length, and the abdomen is yellowish to grey. Like all flies it has only two wings, and the rear pair of wings has turned into tiny **halteres**. These help it to keep its balance in flight. Its big red **compound eyes** are made up of thousands of single eyes.

The housefly is found almost all over the world where people live. In German it is called Stubenfliege, or “living-room fly”, because it often turns up in homes, in the living room. There are especially many near stables, compost heaps and rubbish. There it finds food and places for its eggs.

The housefly has a **sponging proboscis** with which it can only soak up liquid food. Solid food such as sugar it dissolves by putting saliva on it. It likes sweet things, but also rubbish, droppings and spoiled food. With sensory hairs on its feet it can even taste.

The female lays several hundred eggs in damp dung, compost or rubbish. White, legless **maggots** hatch from them. They eat and grow and after a few days pupate in a brown barrel-shaped pupa. In summer warmth the whole development from egg to fly takes only about ten days. That is why there are several **generations** in one summer.

The housefly beats its wings very fast, about 200 times a second, and you hear this as buzzing. Its eyes take in many more pictures per second than ours. That is why it sees a hand swatting at it coming as if in slow motion. With sticky pads on its feet it can even walk on the ceiling and on window panes.

Because houseflies land on droppings and rubbish and afterwards on food, they can pass on **disease germs**. That is why you should cover food and keep rubbish closed. Fly screens on the windows keep them out. For many animals, such as spiders, swallows and other birds, flies are an important food.

begriffe.erklaerung: An eye made up of many small single eyes, typical of insects.
The legless larva of a fly.
Tiny, modified hind wings with which flies keep their balance in flight.
All the animals that are born at about the same time, for example parents or children.

gewusst: Houseflies taste with their feet as soon as they land on something.
To a housefly, a hand racing towards it looks as if it is in slow motion.

teile.einleitung: The black-backed jackal, in German Schabrackenschakal, is a slim, fox-like wild dog from Africa. It gets its name from the dark, saddle-like marking on its back. It lives in savannas and bushland and is a clever hunter and scavenger.
wichtigste: The black-backed jackal lives in eastern and southern Africa.
It feels at home in savannas and bushland.
Its name comes from the dark, saddle-like marking on its back, the Schabracke.
It eats small animals, carrion and fruit, and sometimes catches the young of small antelopes.
Pairs often stay together for life.
Older young animals help their parents to raise the pups.
Leopards can be dangerous to jackals.

abschnitte.text: The black-backed jackal is about as big as a fox and weighs around 6 to 13 kilograms. Its fur is reddish brown, and on its back it has a dark, silvery speckled **saddle**. It has large, pointed ears and a bushy tail with a black tip. It belongs to the **dog** family.

The black-backed jackal lives in two separate areas: in eastern Africa, for example in Kenya and Tanzania, and in southern Africa. It inhabits **savannas**, bushland, dry steppes and even coasts. It tends to avoid forests and deserts. In Namibia it looks for seal carcasses on the coast.

The jackal is an **omnivore**. It hunts mice, hares, birds, lizards and insects and sometimes catches young gazelles or other small antelopes. It often also eats carrion that lions or hyenas leave behind. In addition there are fruit and berries.

Black-backed jackals usually live as a lasting **pair** in a territory. The pups are born in a den, often in an old aardvark burrow. When the pups need solid food, the parents bring up half-digested meat. Older young from earlier litters often stay on as **helpers** and guard and feed the little ones.

Above all **leopards** can be dangerous to it, but eagles, hyenas and pythons also take pups. The species is common and not threatened. Farmers in southern Africa persecute jackals, because they sometimes kill lambs. Jackals can also transmit rabies.

begriffe.erklaerung: A blanket under the saddle, here the dark marking in the fur on the back.
An animal that eats meat and plants.
The area that an animal or pair lives in and defends.
The young of dogs, wolves and jackals.

gewusst: Black-backed jackals communicate with high, wailing howls.
The family with helpers does better: the more helpers, the more pups survive.

teile.einleitung: A wallow is a muddy hollow or puddle in which animals roll about. Wild boar, deer, bison, elephants and rhinoceroses like to bathe in mud. What looks dirty to us is personal care for them.
wichtigste: A wallow is a hollow with mud or water in which animals roll about.
Bison roll in wallows, and so do wild boar and deer.
A mud bath cools the body on hot days.
The layer of mud protects against insects, parasites and sunburn.
Rolling about in the mud is called wallowing.
After wallowing, wild boar rub themselves against trees, so-called rubbing trees.
Wallows are also habitats for frogs, newts and insects.

abschnitte.text: A wallow is a shallow hollow in the ground in which rainwater and mud collect. Animals lie down in it and roll about until their whole body is covered with mud. This behaviour is called **wallowing**. Many wallows are used again and again over the years and become deeper and deeper.

**Wild boar** and domestic pigs are well known for wallowing. Red deer also like to wallow, especially during the rutting season in autumn. In North America **bison** roll in hollows of mud or dust. In Africa and Asia, elephants, rhinoceroses, buffalo and hippopotamuses wallow.

Pigs can hardly sweat, so they cool down in the mud. The drying mud forms a protective layer against flies, horseflies, **ticks** and sunburn. When the mud later falls off, it takes parasites with it. When wallowing, deer also leave behind their scent and in this way show other deer that they are there.

After the mud bath, wild boar rub themselves against a tree nearby, the **rubbing tree**. As a result the bark of these trees is crusted with mud and rubbed smooth up to a certain height. Foresters and hunters can tell from this how big the wild boar in the area are. In Swiss woods you often find such trees next to wallows.

Wallows are small wetlands in the middle of the forest or the prairie. Tadpoles, newts, dragonfly larvae and water beetles live in them. In Switzerland, for example, the rare **yellow-bellied toad** and the alpine newt benefit from such puddles. The old bison wallows in the North American prairie still fill with rainwater today and provide a habitat for many plants and animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal rolling about in the mud.
A tree against which wild boar rub themselves after a mud bath.
Living things such as ticks or lice that live on or in another animal and harm it.
The mating season in deer.

gewusst: Pigs have almost no sweat glands and therefore wallow to avoid overheating.
From the mud on a rubbing tree you can tell how big the wild boar in the area are.

teile.einleitung: The Syrian brown bear is a subspecies of the brown bear that lives in parts of Western Asia. It is also called the Syrian bear and is one of the smaller and lightest forms of brown bear. One of these bears even became famous as a “soldier” in the Second World War.
wichtigste: The Syrian brown bear (Ursus arctos syriacus) is a subspecies of the brown bear.
It lives in parts of Western Asia, for example in Turkey, Iran and the Caucasus.
Its fur is often light, straw-coloured to light brown.
It is one of the smaller brown bears.
It is an omnivore and eats mainly plants, fruit and nuts.
In Syria and Lebanon it is extinct or extremely rare today.

abschnitte.text: The Syrian brown bear is smaller than, for example, the grizzly or the Kodiak bear. Its dense fur is usually **light**, often straw yellow, sandy or light brown, and the legs are sometimes darker. Like all brown bears it has a powerful hump on its shoulders and long **claws** for digging. Males are clearly bigger and heavier than females.

The Syrian brown bear lives in mountain forests and mountain ranges of **Western Asia**. Today it is found mainly in Turkey, Iran, the Caucasus with Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, and in the north of Iraq. In the past it also lived in Syria, in Lebanon and in the area of present-day Israel. There it was wiped out or almost wiped out by hunting and loss of habitat.

The bear is an **omnivore**, but eats mostly plant food. Its menu includes grasses, roots, berries, fruit and nuts. Added to these are insects, larvae, honey and occasionally small mammals or carrion. In autumn it eats its way to a thick layer of fat before it goes into its **winter rest**.

In 1942, Polish soldiers in Iran bought a bear cub, a Syrian brown bear. They called him **Wojtek** and took him along on their journey through the Middle East as far as Italy. He was officially listed as a soldier and is said to have helped to carry crates of ammunition. After the war Wojtek lived in Edinburgh Zoo in Scotland until his death in 1963.

abschnitte.titel: Threats and the link to Switzerland
abschnitte.text: The Syrian brown bear is threatened by poaching, logging and conflicts with farmers. In many countries it is protected, and some animals live in zoos and bear parks. In Switzerland there are no Syrian brown bears in the wild. Here the last native **brown bear** was shot in 1904 in the Lower Engadine, and today bears from the Italian Trentino wander in now and then.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group within an animal species that lives in a particular area and looks a little different.
An animal that eats both plants and animals.
A long sleep in winter in which the body saves energy but does not cool down as much as in hibernation.
An area in the west of Asia, for example Turkey, Iran, Iraq and Syria.

gewusst: The bear Wojtek was given a rank of his own in the Polish army and reportedly liked to drink beer.
Bears in old stories from the Middle East probably mean the Syrian brown bear.
Like all brown bears, the Syrian brown bear can run very fast over short distances despite its size.

teile.einleitung: Seven Sleepers' Day on 27 June is a well-known day in the farmers' calendar. An old farmers' saying says: as the weather is on this day, so it will stay for the next seven weeks. Its name does not come from the animal, but from a Christian legend about seven sleeping brothers.
wichtigste: Seven Sleepers' Day is 27 June.
The name comes from a Christian legend about seven sleeping brothers.
The farmers' saying says that the weather on this day lasts for seven weeks.
The day has nothing to do with the rodent called the dormouse.
Because of a calendar reform, you should really watch the weather at the start of July.
The rule is not entirely wrong, because summer weather often settles in for a longer time around this period.

abschnitte.text: The legend tells of seven young Christians in the city of **Ephesus**, in present-day Turkey. Around the year 251, they are said to have hidden in a cave from the persecution of Christians by the Roman emperor Decius. The cave was walled up, and the seven brothers fell asleep. Only about 200 years later are they said to have woken up again, when Christianity had long been permitted. That is why they are called the **Seven Sleepers**.

In memory of this legend, Seven Sleepers' Day is celebrated on 27 June. In the Middle Ages it was entered in the calendar, and farmers knew it well. Later the day was linked with the weather, because it falls in the middle of the important time for the **harvest**. The Seven Sleepers are also mentioned in Islam, where they are called the People of the Cave.

A well-known **farmers' saying** runs roughly: if it is fine on Seven Sleepers' Day, it stays fine for seven weeks, and if it rains, it stays wet for seven weeks. Farmers' sayings are old weather proverbs based on long observation. They used to help farmers to plan their work in the field. Not all farmers' sayings are true, but some have a true core.

At the end of June and the start of July, it is often decided in central Europe which **weather pattern** will shape high summer. If the jet stream, a strong wind at great height, lies favourably, it often stays sunny for a long time, and otherwise low pressure systems keep coming. Weather researchers have found that in some regions the rule is roughly right in about two years out of three. What matters is not a single day, but the weather over several days around this time.

In 1582 Pope Gregory XIII introduced a new **calendar**, and ten days were skipped in the process. The farmers' saying, however, is older than this reform. By the old calendar, Seven Sleepers' Day would today correspond to about 7 July. Anyone who wants to test the rule should therefore rather watch the weather in the first week of July.

begriffe.erklaerung: An old saying that derives a forecast from weather observations.
An old tale about saints or special events that is not firmly proved.
A very strong wind at great height that influences the weather in Europe.
A change in the reckoning of time, such as the introduction of the Gregorian calendar in 1582.

gewusst: The rodent called the dormouse gets its name from its long winter sleep, not from Seven Sleepers' Day.
In Ephesus a grotto is shown to this day that is said to be the cave of the Seven Sleepers.
Switzerland did not adopt the new calendar of 1582 everywhere at the same time, and some Protestant places changed only much later.

teile.einleitung: The snow leopard is a large big cat that lives in the highest mountains of Central Asia. With its dense, pale grey fur and very long tail, it is perfectly adapted to cold and rock. Because it is so shy, it is often called the ghost of the mountains.
wichtigste: The snow leopard lives in the high mountains of Central Asia, for example in the Himalayas.
Its very long tail helps with balancing and serves as a warming blanket.
Its large, broad paws work like snowshoes.
The strong, somewhat longer hind legs make it a good jumper.
It cannot really roar like a lion.
Important prey animals are the bharal and ibex.
Researchers often observe it with camera traps.

abschnitte.text: The snow leopard has dense, smoky grey to cream coloured fur with dark ring-shaped spots, the **rosettes**. It usually weighs about 25 to 55 kilograms. Its bushy **tail** is almost as long as the body. It helps with balancing on rock, and when sleeping the snow leopard wraps it round its nose and paws like a blanket. Its paws are large, broad and hairy, so that it does not sink into the snow.

Snow leopards live in the high mountains of Central Asia, for example in the **Himalayas**, the Altai, the Tian Shan and the Pamir. They occur in twelve countries, including China, Mongolia, Nepal and India. Mostly they live between about 3,000 and 5,500 metres above sea level. There it is cold and rocky, and the air is thin.

The snow leopard hunts mainly larger hoofed animals such as the **bharal**, or blue sheep, and the Siberian ibex. In addition there are marmots, pikas and birds. It stalks its prey and then pounces. With its strong, somewhat longer hind legs it manages long leaps. Sometimes it also kills livestock such as sheep and goats, and then herders lose animals and are often angry.

Snow leopards mostly live alone. After mating in late winter, the female raises her young in a **rock cave** or a crevice. Mostly two to three young are born, which are blind and helpless at first. The young stay with the mother for about one and a half to two years and learn to hunt in that time.

Although it belongs to the big cats, the snow leopard cannot really roar like a lion or a tiger. Instead it hisses, growls and mews. Typical too is a friendly snort that is called **chuffing**. With scent marks on rocks, snow leopards show one another where they are travelling.

There are only a few thousand snow leopards left in the wild. They are poached for their fur and their bones, and some are killed by herders. Climate change is also altering their habitat. Because they are so shy, they are often studied with **camera traps**. In Switzerland you can see snow leopards, for example, at Zurich Zoo and Basel Zoo.

begriffe.erklaerung: Ring-shaped dark spots in the fur of cats.
A camera that is triggered automatically when an animal moves.
The illegal hunting of protected animals.
A friendly snort with which some big cats greet one another.

gewusst: A snow leopard can jump several metres from a standing start.
The snow leopard can bring down prey that weighs about three times as much as itself.

teile.einleitung: Fresh water is water that contains hardly any salt, as in streams, rivers, lakes and groundwater. For many animals it is the most important habitat, for example for the whitefish in the Swiss lakes. Although the Earth is a blue planet, only a very small part of its water is fresh water.
wichtigste: Fresh water contains less than one gram of salt per litre.
Only about 2.5 to 3 per cent of all the water on Earth is fresh water, and most of that is frozen as ice.
The whitefish of the Swiss lakes live in fresh water.
A distinction is made between flowing waters such as streams and rivers and still waters such as lakes and ponds.
Freshwater animals constantly have to get rid of excess water from their bodies.
Switzerland is called the “water tower of Europe” because of its many springs, lakes and glaciers.

abschnitte.text: In seawater about 35 grams of salt per litre are dissolved on average. **Fresh water**, on the other hand, contains less than one gram of salt per litre, which is why it does not taste salty. Where rivers flow into the sea, the two mix to form **brackish water**. Fresh water comes mainly from rain and snow, because when water evaporates, the salt stays behind in the sea.

Switzerland has about 1500 lakes and countless streams and rivers. Big rivers such as the **Rhine**, the Rhone and the Inn rise here. A large part of the fresh water is stored in glaciers, lakes and groundwater. That is why Switzerland is called the **water tower of Europe**.

In Swiss waters live fish such as **whitefish**, brown trout, pike, perch and grayling. Added to these are many smaller animals such as freshwater shrimps, water snails, dragonfly larvae and caddisfly larvae. Mammals such as the beaver and birds such as the great crested grebe or the kingfisher also depend on fresh water. Many insects spend their youth as larvae in the water and only live on land as adults.

The body of a freshwater fish is saltier than the water around it. That is why water constantly seeps into its body through the skin and gills, which is called **osmosis**. The fish therefore hardly drinks and passes a lot of very dilute urine. Sea fish have the opposite problem, which is why most fish can live in only one of the two kinds of water.

Fresh water is scarce and valuable, also as drinking water for people. Pollution from fertiliser, waste water and microplastics harms the animals. Straightened rivers and dams destroy spawning grounds, and warmer water troubles cold-loving fish such as the grayling. In Switzerland, many streams and rivers are therefore being **restored to a natural state**, which means rebuilt to be close to nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water with very little dissolved salt, for example in rivers and lakes.
A mixture of fresh water and seawater, for example at river mouths.
Water moves through a thin skin from the side with less salt to the side with more salt.
A built-up waterway is made more natural again.

gewusst: Salmon and eels can change between fresh water and the sea because their bodies can adjust.
Most of the Earth’s fresh water is locked up in the ice of Antarctica and Greenland.
The water from many Swiss taps is so clean that it can be drunk straight from springs and groundwater without treatment.

teile.einleitung: The common earthworm, in German the Tauwurm or “dew worm”, is one of the most common large earthworms in Switzerland and in the whole of Europe. It can grow up to about 30 centimetres long and digs deep, vertical tunnels into the soil. At night it comes up to the surface to pull leaves into its burrow.
wichtigste: The common earthworm (Lumbricus terrestris) is a large species of earthworm.
Fully grown, it reaches up to about 30 centimetres long.
It digs vertical burrows that can reach two metres and deeper into the soil.
It has its German name because it comes up to the surface on damp, dewy nights.
It eats dead leaves and turns them into fertile humus.
Common earthworms are hermaphrodites, and each animal is male and female at the same time.

abschnitte.text: The common earthworm has a long, round body of over a hundred **segments**. The front end is reddish brown and strong, the rear end flatter and lighter. In adult worms you can see a thick, light ring, the **girdle** or clitellum. It has no eyes, ears or lungs, and breathes through its moist skin.

Common earthworms dig vertical **living burrows** that often reach two to three metres deep. In them they live for many years in the same place. At night they stretch the front of the body out of the burrow and pull leaves into it, while the rear end stays anchored in the burrow. In the morning you often see small piles of leaves and small piles of droppings over the burrow entrances on meadows.

The common earthworm eats dead leaves and soil with plant remains. Its droppings are especially nutrient-rich **humus**, which makes the soil fertile. Through its tunnels, air and rainwater get deep into the soil, and plant roots grow more easily. Farmers and gardeners are therefore glad to see many earthworms.

Common earthworms are **hermaphrodites**, but they still need a partner. On warm, damp nights two worms lie side by side at the surface and exchange seed. After that the girdle forms a slimy sheath from which a small **cocoon** with an egg arises. After a few weeks a tiny young worm hatches from it.

Common earthworms are eaten by blackbirds, hedgehogs, badgers, foxes and moles. The mole even lays in stores by paralysing worms with a bite and keeping them in its burrow. Anglers use common earthworms as **bait** for fish. When a worm is cut in two, by the way, two worms do not result, and usually at most the front part survives.

begriffe.erklaerung: A worm that lives in the soil and loosens and fertilises the earth.
A living thing that has both male and female sex organs.
A thickened ring in adult earthworms from which the cocoon arises.
A protective sheath in which an egg develops.

gewusst: Charles Darwin wrote his last book in 1881 about earthworms and showed how over decades they turn over whole layers of soil.
Under a meadow, several hundred earthworms can live per square metre.
A common earthworm can live for several years.

teile.einleitung: Play behaviour is the name for everything that people and animals do out of joy, without it serving a serious purpose straight away. Young cats chase balls of wool, dogs romp and children play tag. But behind the fun there is much more, because when you play, you learn for life.
wichtigste: Play occurs mainly in mammals and birds.
Young animals play much more than adult animals.
In play, animals practise movements that they later need for hunting or fleeing.
Play strengthens friendship and the rank order in a group.
Dogs invite play with a bow, the front of the body flat on the ground and the rear end up.
In play, animals bite only with restraint, so that nobody is hurt.
Humans too learn rules, skill and cooperation when they play.

abschnitte.text: Play is behaviour that happens voluntarily and brings joy. It often looks like serious behaviour, for example like fighting or hunting, but is only a **fun fight**. Typical is that movements are exaggerated, repeated or shown in an unusual order. An animal plays above all when it is well fed, healthy and relaxed.

So that a play fight is not mistaken for a real fight, animals send **play signals**. Dogs put the front of the body flat on the ground and stretch the rear end up, which is an invitation to others to play. Chimpanzees show a play face with an open mouth, but without bared teeth. In humans, laughter shows that it is all just fun.

In play, young animals train their **muscles**, their balance and their skill. Young cats practise stalking and pouncing, and young roe deer practise quick dodging. At the same time the animals learn how hard they may bite and how to behave in a group. Researchers suspect that play also helps to cope better with surprises.

Especially playful are otters, which make slides in the water or in the snow. Ravens and **keas**, parrots from New Zealand, play with objects and sometimes slide down snowy slopes. Dolphins blow air rings and play with them. Adult dogs, horses and monkeys also like to go on playing.

For children, play is the most important way of learning. In role play they practise everyday situations, and in ball games team spirit and **fairness**. Games played together need rules that everyone keeps to. Experts recommend that children have time for free play every day.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sign with which an animal shows another that it would like to play.
The ability to bite only gently in play.
A typical dog posture with the front of the body low and the rear end stretched up.
A game in which you pretend to be someone else.

gewusst: When tickled and when playing, rats make sounds that sound like laughter, but are too high for humans to hear.
In a play fight, a stronger dog deliberately lets a weaker one win now and then.
Ravens have been observed lying on their backs and sliding down snowy slopes.

teile.einleitung: The harbour seal is a seal with a round head, large dark eyes and long whiskers. You often see it on sandbanks in the Wadden Sea, where it warms itself in the sun. In the water it is a skilful swimmer and fish hunter.
wichtigste: The scientific name of the harbour seal is Phoca vitulina.
Harbour seals belong to the seals, which are also called pinnipeds.
Because of their diet they count among the carnivores or predators.
Their fur is mostly grey brown with dark spots.
With their long whiskers they sense fishes in the water.
Harbour seal pups can swim shortly after birth.
A harbour seal can live up to 30 years.

abschnitte.text: The **harbour seal** has a round head that is a little reminiscent of a dog. Its fur is mostly **grey brown with dark spots**, but the colour varies a great deal. Males grow to almost 2 metres long and weigh over 100 kilograms. On the outside it has no ear flaps, only small openings, so it belongs to the **true seals**.

Harbour seals live on the coasts of the North Atlantic and the North Pacific. In Europe they are common, for example, in the **Wadden Sea** of the North Sea. At low tide they lie on sandbanks, rest and warm themselves in the sun. Harbour seals sometimes even sleep floating in the water.

Harbour seals are **carnivores** and live mainly on fishes such as herring, flatfishes or sand eels. With their long **whiskers** they sense the fine water movements that swimming fishes make. In this way they find prey even in murky water or in the dark. When diving, they close their nose and ears and slow down their heartbeat.

In the Wadden Sea the young are born in summer on a sandbank. A **harbour seal pup** can swim shortly after birth, because at the next high tide the sandbank is flooded. The mother suckles it for only three to four weeks with very fat-rich milk. A pup that has lost its mother and calls loudly is called a **howler**, in German Heuler.

Among the natural enemies of the harbour seal is the **killer whale**. In the past, harbour seals were hunted heavily, but today they are protected in many countries. In 1988 and 2002, thousands of harbour seals in the North Sea died of a viral disease. Anyone who finds a young harbour seal on the beach should keep their distance and notify the experts at a **seal rescue centre**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Collective name for seals whose limbs are changed into flippers.
A young harbour seal that has been separated from its mother and calls for her.
A shallow coastal sea that partly dries out at low tide.
Seals without external ear flaps, to which the harbour seal belongs.

gewusst: On land the harbour seal moves along on its belly, because it cannot turn its hind flippers under its body.
Harbour seals can slow their heartbeat greatly when diving in order to save oxygen.

teile.einleitung: Partial migrants are bird species in which some of the animals fly south in autumn, while the others stay in their breeding area. Typical partial migrants in Switzerland are the blackbird, the robin and the chaffinch. Which bird goes and which stays depends on its genes, its age, its sex and the weather.
wichtigste: Partial migrants are birds of which some migrate and some stay.
Well-known partial migrants are the blackbird, robin, chaffinch, starling and blackcap.
Often it is rather the females and young birds that leave, while older males stay.
Partial migrants stand between the resident birds and the migratory birds.
Thanks to milder winters, more birds now stay in Switzerland over winter.
The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach uses rings and transmitters to study how birds migrate.

abschnitte.text: In a **partial migrant**, not all birds of a species behave the same way. Some leave the breeding area in autumn and spend the winter in the south, for example in southern France, Spain or North Africa. The others stay there all winter. Partial migrants are therefore an in-between form between **resident birds** and **migratory birds**.

abschnitte.titel: Resident birds, migratory birds and wanderers
abschnitte.text: **Resident birds** such as the house sparrow, woodpeckers and nuthatches stay in their area all year round. **Migratory birds** such as the swift, barn swallow and cuckoo leave Switzerland every autumn and fly as far as Africa. Wandering birds only roam short distances in winter, depending on where they find food. In many species the transitions are gradual.

Whether a bird migrates is partly fixed in its **genes**. Age, sex and food supply also play a part. Often young birds and females are the ones to leave, while experienced males stay to take the best territories in spring. The researcher Carl Linnaeus therefore called the chaffinch the “bachelor”, because in Sweden it was mainly males that stayed behind in winter.
