In winter you often see robins, blackbirds and chaffinches in Switzerland, but they are not always the same birds as in summer. Some native birds have left, while **winter visitors** from Scandinavia or eastern Europe have arrived. A robin at the bird table can therefore come from Sweden. We know this thanks to **ringing**: birds are given a small ring with a number on the leg.

Because winters are getting milder, more birds now stay in their breeding area. In the **blackcap** a new migration route has even developed: many animals from central Europe no longer spend the winter in Spain but in Great Britain. Partial migrants can adapt to changes faster than pure migratory birds. The **Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach** in the canton of Lucerne has been watching such changes for many decades.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird species in which only some of the animals leave in winter.
A bird that stays in the same area all year round.
A bird that travels back and forth every year between its breeding area and its winter quarters.
Marking birds with a numbered leg ring in order to study their routes.

gewusst: The scientific name of the chaffinch, Fringilla coelebs, means “unmarried finch”, because in winter often only the males stay in the north.
Blackbirds used to be regarded as shy woodland birds and only became town dwellers in the 19th century, and in towns they often no longer migrate at all.
Whether a young blackcap flies south-west or north-west is fixed in its genes.

teile.einleitung: The Sri Lankan elephant is a subspecies of the Asian elephant that lives on the island of Sri Lanka in the Indian Ocean. It is the largest subspecies of the Asian elephant. For the people of Sri Lanka it is an important symbol and takes part in many festivals.
wichtigste: The Sri Lankan elephant lives only on the island of Sri Lanka, south of India.
It is the largest subspecies of the Asian elephant.
Typical features are lighter, pink-spotted patches on the ears, face and trunk.
Only very few bulls have large tusks.
About 6000 wild elephants live in Sri Lanka (count of 2011).
The subspecies is seriously endangered, mainly because of the loss of its habitat.
At the Esala Perahera festival in Kandy, decorated elephants walk through the city.

abschnitte.text: Sri Lankan elephants have dark skin with light, pink patches without **pigment** on the ears, forehead, trunk and belly. Bulls can reach a shoulder height of up to three metres and weigh several tonnes. Like all Asian elephants, they have smaller ears than African elephants and an arched back. It is especially striking that only a small share of the bulls have real **tusks**.

The elephants live in forests, grasslands and scrubland in the lowlands of Sri Lanka, mostly in the drier north and east. Well-known protected areas are **Yala National Park** and Minneriya National Park. They need a lot of water and like to stay near lakes and reservoirs. A grown elephant eats well over 100 kilograms of grass, leaves, bark and fruit every day.

Females and young live in family groups led by an experienced **matriarch**. Adult bulls usually wander alone or in small bachelor groups. In the dry season, several hundred elephants often gather on the shore of a large reservoir in Minneriya National Park. This event is called “The Gathering” and is regarded as one of the largest gatherings of elephants in Asia.

Elephants have played an important part in the culture of Sri Lanka for over 2000 years. At the Buddhist festival **Esala Perahera** in Kandy, splendidly decorated elephants carry a casket with a sacred relic through the streets every year. At the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage, founded in 1975, orphaned young elephants are raised. Tamed elephants were also used in the past for work in the forest.

The greatest danger is the loss of habitat, because forests are cleared for fields, villages and roads. This often leads to **conflicts** between people and elephants, which wander into fields and eat the crops. Every year hundreds of elephants and also many people die in Sri Lanka in such encounters. Protective fences, corridors between protected areas and education are meant to help people and elephants live together more peacefully.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group within a species that differs in its features and where it lives.
Lengthened front teeth of elephants, made of ivory.
The oldest and most experienced female, who leads an elephant herd.
A place where young animals without a mother are raised.

gewusst: Among Sri Lankan elephants only a few bulls have tusks, while among African elephants almost all of them do.
Elephants can communicate with one another over several kilometres using deep sounds that people cannot hear.
In relation to its area, Sri Lanka has one of the highest densities of elephants in Asia.

teile.einleitung: The Simmental Fleckvieh is a well-known Swiss cattle breed with brown and white patches and a mostly white head. It comes from the Simmental in the Bernese Oberland and is today one of the most widespread cattle breeds in the world.
wichtigste: The Simmental is a Swiss cattle breed from the Simmental in the canton of Bern.
Its coat is reddish brown to yellowish and patched with white, and the head is mostly white.
They give both a lot of milk and good meat.
Such breeds are called dual-purpose breeds.
Simmental cattle were exported to many countries as early as the 19th century.
Today there are Simmental cattle on all continents.
In Germany and Austria the breed is called Fleckvieh.

abschnitte.text: Simmental cows have a brown and white patched coat, with the brown ranging from pale yellow to a strong reddish brown. Typical is the **white head**, and often the belly and legs are also white. They are large, strong animals: a cow weighs about 650 to 800 kilograms, and a bull clearly over a tonne. The horns are removed in many animals or do not grow naturally.

The breed comes from the **Simmental**, a valley in the Bernese Oberland through which the Simme flows. The farmers there had bred strong cattle for Alpine farming for centuries. In the past the animals were also harnessed in front of carts and ploughs. In the 19th century, Simmental cattle were sold to many countries of Europe and later to America, Africa and Australia.

Simmental cattle are a **dual-purpose breed**: they give a lot of milk and at the same time put on a lot of meat. In Switzerland, cheese is also made from their milk, for example Emmentaler or Gruyère. The calves grow quickly and are popular as meat animals. This mixture makes the breed especially valuable for many farmers.

Simmental cattle are among the most widespread **cattle breeds** in the world. In Germany and Austria they are called Fleckvieh, and there it is the most common breed of cattle. In Switzerland many Simmental cattle were crossed with Red Holstein cows, from which the **Swiss Fleckvieh** arose. The pure, original animals are today called Original Simmental.

Together with the Brown Swiss and the Holstein cows, Simmental cattle are among the most important cattle breeds of Switzerland. You see them especially often in the canton of Bern, in western Switzerland and on the Alps. At the **descent from the Alp** in autumn, the cows are decorated with flowers and large bells. Many farming families are proud of their Simmental cattle and show them at cattle shows.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of domestic animals with common, inherited features.
An animal breed that is bred for two purposes, such as milk and meat.
The keeping of cattle on mountain pastures in summer.
An exhibition at which farmers show their finest animals and have them judged.

gewusst: Simmental cattle can be found today from Canada to South Africa and Australia.
In Germany the Fleckvieh, that is, the descendant of the Simmental, is the most common breed of cattle.
In the past, Simmental oxen pulled heavy carts and ploughs.

teile.einleitung: Tailed amphibians, in German Schwanzlurche, are amphibians that keep a tail even as adults. They include the salamanders and the newts, for example the alpine newt. They live partly in water and partly on land and can regrow lost body parts.
wichtigste: Tailed amphibians form an order of their own within the amphibians.
They include salamanders and newts, such as the alpine newt.
About 800 species are known worldwide, most of them in the Northern Hemisphere.
They have an elongated body, four short legs and a moist skin.
Their larvae breathe with tufts of gills and get the front legs first.
Tailed amphibians can regrow legs and even parts of organs.
In Switzerland all amphibians are protected.

abschnitte.text: At first sight, **tailed amphibians** look like lizards, but they are amphibians. Their skin is bare, moist and without scales. They breathe through lungs and in addition through the skin. Unlike frogs and toads, they never lose their tail.

People roughly distinguish **salamanders**, which mostly live on land, and **newts**, which go into the water at mating time. The largest tailed amphibian is the Chinese giant salamander, which can grow well over a metre long. The Mexican **axolotl** stays a larva with gills for its whole life and still reproduces. Most species live in North America, Europe and Asia.

Most tailed amphibians lay their eggs in the water. Female newts wrap each egg singly in a leaf of a water plant. The larvae have **tufts of gills** on the outside of the head and get the front legs first. The fire salamander puts fully formed larvae into streams, and the alpine salamander even gives birth to fully developed young.

In Switzerland live, among others, the fire salamander, the alpine salamander, the alpine newt, the palmate newt, the smooth newt and the great crested newt. The **alpine newt** has a bright orange, unspotted belly, and the male is coloured blue at mating time. It occurs from the lowlands to over 2,000 metres. The black alpine salamander lives in the mountains and needs no water for its young.

Many tailed amphibians are threatened because ponds and wetlands are disappearing. Roads cut across their migration routes between winter quarters and spawning waters. In addition, an introduced **skin fungus**, called the salamander eater, threatens many species in Europe. In Switzerland all amphibians are protected, and volunteers help with amphibian fences along roads.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals that live mostly in water and on land, for example frogs and newts.
Feathery gills on the outside of the head with which larvae breathe in water.
The regrowing of lost body parts.
The young stage that often lives in water and looks different from the adult animal.

gewusst: A newt can completely regrow a severed leg, including bones and toes.
At high altitudes the alpine salamander is pregnant for up to three or four years.

teile.einleitung: Spiracles, called “Stigmen” in German, are small breathing openings in the skin of insects, millipedes and other arthropods. Air flows through them into a fine system of tubes in the body. In this way these animals breathe without any lungs at all.
wichtigste: A spiracle (in German “Stigma”) is a breathing opening in insects and other arthropods.
Millipedes take in air through spiracles.
The spiracles are usually on the sides of the body.
From the spiracles, fine tubes called tracheae lead through the whole body.
Many insects can open and close their spiracles.
This way of breathing limits the size of insects.
In botany, “stigma” means something different, namely the stigma of a flower.

abschnitte.text: The German word Stigma comes from Greek and means dot or mark. In zoology it is the name for the tiny **breathing openings** in the outer covering of arthropods. They are also called breathing holes. In caterpillars they are easy to see as small dark dots on the side of each body ring.

Through the spiracles, air gets into a network of fine tubes, the **tracheae**. These branch out further and further until they reach right up to the cells. The oxygen therefore does not have to be carried by blood as it is in us. Many insects have small flaps or muscles with which they close the spiracles so that they do not dry out.

Insects usually have up to ten pairs of spiracles, two on the chest and up to eight on the abdomen. **Millipedes** and centipedes also breathe through spiracles and tracheae. Many spiders also have spiracles, which lead to book lungs or tracheae. Grasshoppers and bees pump with their abdomen to exchange the air faster.

Water insects have special tricks. The larvae of **mosquitoes** hang at the surface of the water and breathe through a breathing tube at the rear end. The great diving beetle takes an air bubble under its wing cases with it when it dives. In this way air reaches its spiracles even when it is under water.

Because oxygen travels only slowly through the tracheae, this kind of breathing works well only in small animals. About 300 million years ago, in the **Carboniferous**, the air contained more oxygen than today. At that time there lived giant dragonflies with a wingspan of over 60 centimetres. Today such giants are no longer possible.

In botany the sticky tip of the pistil of a flower is also called a stigma, in German **Narbe**. Pollen grains stick there. In many insects there is also a dark mark on the wing that is likewise called a stigma. Which meaning is intended can be told from the context.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fine, branching windpipes in the body of insects and millipedes.
Animals with a hard outer skeleton and jointed legs, for example insects, spiders and crustaceans.
The topmost, sticky part of the pistil of a flower, which catches the pollen.

gewusst: Insects have no blood that carries oxygen, and the air reaches the cells directly through the spiracles.
Because of the higher oxygen content of the air, there were dragonflies as big as crows about 300 million years ago.

teile.einleitung: A sniffer dog is a dog that has been trained to track down particular smells with its nose. It finds drugs, explosives, missing people or even illnesses. This is possible because dogs can smell much better than people.
wichtigste: Dogs have many more smell cells in the nose than humans.
Sniffer dogs can filter the tiniest traces of particular substances out of a complex mixture of smells.
Police, customs, army and rescue services use sniffer dogs.
In Switzerland, avalanche dogs search for people buried in the snow.
Research is studying how dogs can recognise illnesses such as cancer by smell.
Sniffer dogs are trained with rewards and play.
Breeds often used are German shepherds, Malinois and Labrador retrievers.

abschnitte.text: A human has about five million **smell cells**, a German shepherd about 200 million. In addition, the part of the brain that processes smells is much larger in the dog. When sniffing, the dog breathes in short, quick breaths so that a lot of air sweeps past the smell cells. In this way it can notice smells that are completely unnoticeable to us.

abschnitte.titel: At customs and with the police
abschnitte.text: At **customs**, sniffer dogs search suitcases, parcels and vehicles for drugs, money or smuggled goods. The police use dogs to find explosives, weapons or the traces of offenders. A good sniffer dog can recognise a particular smell even when it is covered by many other smells. When it has found something, it usually signals it by sitting or lying down calmly.

In the Swiss Alps, **avalanche dogs** are especially important. They smell people buried under several metres of snow and can search an area much faster than many helpers with probes. After earthquakes too, rescue dogs search the rubble for survivors. In Switzerland, for example, Alpine Rescue Switzerland and the association REDOG train such dogs.

Researchers are studying whether dogs, with their exceptionally fine sense of smell, can help with **medical diagnoses**. In studies, dogs have recognised certain kinds of cancer in the breath or urine of patients. Other dogs warn people with diabetes when their blood sugar falls dangerously. During the Covid pandemic, dogs were tested that were supposed to recognise infected people by their sweat.

Sniffer dogs learn their job through play: they look for a particular smell and get a toy or food as a **reward**. The training usually lasts several months, and the dog and its handler form a fixed team. Not every dog is suitable, and what matters is stamina, curiosity and enjoyment of the work. Besides working dogs there are also truffle dogs, which search the forest for expensive fungi.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sense cells in the nose that notice smells.
The agreed sign with which a sniffer dog reports a find.
Searching for a particular person by their own smell.
A dog that works for the police, customs, army or border protection.

gewusst: A dog can smell with each nostril separately and so work out from which direction a smell comes.
The bloodhound is regarded as one of the best tracking dogs and can follow trails that are days old.
In the past in Switzerland, the St Bernards of the Great St Bernard Pass helped in the search for lost people in the snow.

teile.einleitung: A keystone species is a species of animal or plant that is much more important for its habitat than its numbers would suggest. If it disappears, the whole ecosystem changes, just as an arch collapses when you remove the keystone. Well-known examples are the beaver, the wolf and the sea otter.
wichtigste: A keystone species has a disproportionately large influence on its ecosystem.
Many other species depend on it directly or indirectly.
If it disappears, the whole habitat changes greatly.
The technical term in English is keystone species.
The term was coined by the American ecologist Robert Paine in the 1960s.
Examples are the beaver, the wolf, the sea otter and the elephant.
Protecting keystone species helps many other species at the same time.

abschnitte.text: A **keystone species** is a species that plays an especially important role in an ecosystem. Its influence is much greater than you would expect from its numbers or size. The name **keystone** comes from the top stone in a stone arch. If you take it out, the whole arch falls down. In the same way, a habitat is thrown out of balance when a keystone species is missing.

In the 1960s the ecologist **Robert Paine** studied rocky coasts on the west coast of the USA. There he removed a starfish that eats mussels. Afterwards the mussels spread strongly and pushed out many other species. The variety in this habitat decreased clearly. In this way Paine showed how important a single species can be.

A good example from Switzerland is the **beaver**. With its dams it holds back streams and creates ponds and wetlands. There dragonflies, amphibians, fishes and birds find new habitats. The beaver was wiped out in Switzerland in the 19th century and was reintroduced from 1956. Species that rebuild their habitat in this way are also called **ecosystem engineers**.

In **Yellowstone National Park** in the USA, wolves were reintroduced in 1995. Afterwards the behaviour of the deer changed, and on some riverbanks more young trees grew again. Sea otters eat sea urchins and so protect kelp forests in the sea. African elephants keep savannas open by pushing over bushes and small trees. Plants such as fig trees can also be keystone species, because they provide food for many animals.

Anyone who protects keystone species protects many other species at the same time. That is why they are often especially at the centre of **nature conservation**. However, it is not always easy to tell which species is a keystone species. Often you notice only when it has disappeared. That is why it is wise to preserve the whole variety of species.

begriffe.erklaerung: A habitat with all the living things that live and work together in it.
The top stone that holds a stone arch together.
A species that greatly rebuilds its habitat, like the beaver.
The variety of different animal and plant species in an area.

gewusst: Even very small animals can be keystone species, for example bees as pollinators or ants.
A keystone species is often not common at all, and a single pack of wolves can influence a large area.

teile.einleitung: The killer whale, also called the orca, is a black and white marine mammal with a tall dorsal fin. Although it is called a whale, it belongs to the dolphin family and is its largest member. It is a clever hunter that lives in family groups.
wichtigste: The killer whale, or orca, is called Orcinus orca scientifically.
It actually belongs to the dolphin family and is the largest dolphin.
Males grow to about 9 metres long and weigh several tonnes.
Orcas live in fixed family groups led by old females.
They hunt fishes, seals, penguins and even large whales.
Killer whales are among the natural enemies of young blue whales.
Orcas occur in all the world's oceans, most commonly in cold waters.

abschnitte.text: The **killer whale** is black with a white belly and a white patch behind the eye. The **dorsal fin** of the males is tall and straight like a sword and can reach almost 2 metres. Females are smaller and have a curved fin. As a **toothed whale**, the orca has strong, cone-shaped teeth.

Orcas live in all the oceans of the world, from the polar seas to tropical waters. They are most common in cool seas, for example off Norway, Iceland, Canada and in the Antarctic. Some groups stay in one area, others travel far. Depending on the region, researchers distinguish different **ecotypes** with their own prey and their own behaviour.

Killer whales are **apex predators**, and they have no natural enemies. Depending on the group they eat herring, salmon, seals, penguins or sharks. Together they even attack young blue whales and other large whales. In the Antarctic they make waves in order to wash seals off ice floes.

Orcas live in **pods**, that is, family groups that are usually led by an experienced mother or grandmother. The young often stay with their mother for their whole life. Each group has sounds of its own, almost like a **dialect**. For orientation, orcas use echolocation with clicking sounds.

The English name killer whale sounds dangerous, but free-living orcas practically never attack people. In the past many animals were caught for dolphinariums, which is strongly criticised today. Orcas are threatened by environmental toxins, noise in the sea and lack of prey. Females can live over 50 years, and some even considerably longer.

begriffe.erklaerung: A whale with teeth, for example a dolphin, orca or sperm whale.
A hunter at the top of the food chain that has no natural enemies.
Orientation by sounds whose echo comes back.
A group within a species that has adapted to a particular way of life.

gewusst: Female orcas stop having young after about 40 years, but still help their families for a long time.
An orca group passes on its knowledge of hunting tricks from generation to generation.

teile.einleitung: Sheep's milk is the milk of sheep. It is especially rich in fat and protein and is therefore very good for making cheese. Famous cheeses such as feta, Roquefort or Pecorino are made from sheep's milk.
wichtigste: Sheep's milk comes from dairy sheep, which are milked in a similar way to cows.
It contains clearly more fat and protein than cow's milk.
Cheeses such as feta, Roquefort, Pecorino and Manchego are made from sheep's milk.
A sheep gives much less milk than a cow.
Around the Mediterranean, sheep's milk has a long tradition.
In Switzerland too there is sheep's milk, sheep's yoghurt and sheep's cheese.

abschnitte.text: Sheep's milk is white and tastes somewhat stronger and sweeter than cow's milk. It contains about 6 to 7 per cent **fat** and around 5 to 6 per cent **protein**, so almost twice as much as cow's milk. That is why it is thicker and creamier. From a litre of sheep's milk you get clearly more cheese than from a litre of cow's milk.

Breeds such as the **East Friesian dairy sheep** or the French Lacaune sheep give especially much milk. A sheep usually gives about 1 to 3 litres a day, and a dairy cow often 20 litres and more. Milking takes place after the lambs are born, by hand or with a milking machine. A sheep has two teats, a cow four.

**Feta** from Greece is a white brined cheese made from sheep's milk, often with some goat's milk. Roquefort from France is a blue cheese that matures in rock caves. Pecorino from Italy and Manchego from Spain are hard sheep's cheeses. Ricotta, too, is often made from sheep's milk.

Sheep's milk is especially common in the countries around the **Mediterranean** and in the Near East, for example in Greece, Turkey, Italy and Spain. There people have kept sheep for thousands of years, which also manage on poor pastures. Production is also large in China and India. Mostly the milk is not drunk, but made into cheese and yoghurt.

In Switzerland, sheep's milk is rather a speciality. A few farms keep dairy sheep and make **sheep's yoghurt**, fresh cheese and sheep's cheese. Some people who do not tolerate cow's milk well tolerate sheep's milk better, but that is not so for everyone. With a real milk protein allergy, sheep's milk too is usually not suitable.

begriffe.erklaerung: A nutrient that the body needs to build muscles.
Salt water in which, for example, feta is kept.
Cheese with an edible blue green mould inside.
A breed of sheep that is kept mainly for its milk.

gewusst: Real feta may be made only in Greece and must consist for the most part of sheep's milk.
Roquefort is one of the oldest protected cheeses of France and matures in caves under Mount Combalou.

teile.einleitung: The mountain hare is a hare of the Alps and the far north that changes its coat according to the season. In summer it is grey brown, and in winter snow white and so perfectly camouflaged in the snow. In Switzerland it lives in the mountains above the tree line.
wichtigste: The mountain hare changes its fur colour to white in winter in order to camouflage itself.
In summer its fur is grey brown.
The tips of the ears stay black all year round.
Its broad, hairy hind feet work like snowshoes.
In Switzerland it lives in the Alps, mostly between about 1,300 and 3,000 metres.
It eats grasses, herbs, twigs and bark.
Climate change is causing it trouble.

abschnitte.text: The mountain hare is somewhat smaller than the brown hare and usually weighs about 2 to 3.5 kilograms. Its ears are shorter than in the brown hare and have **black tips**. In summer the fur is grey brown, and in winter almost completely white. The hind feet are broad and densely haired. In this way it sinks less into the snow, rather as with **snowshoes**.

Twice a year the mountain hare changes its coat, which is called **moulting**. In autumn a dense white winter coat grows, and in spring a grey brown summer coat. The change is triggered mainly by the **length of the day**, not by the snow. If, because of climate change, there is less snow, a white hare sometimes sits clearly visible on brown ground. Then enemies can easily spot it.

Mountain hares live in northern Europe, northern Asia and in the Alps. In Switzerland they mostly live between about 1,300 and 3,000 metres above sea level. They like open mountain forests, dwarf shrub heaths and Alpine pastures. The mountain hares of the Alps are an **ice age relic**: after the last ice age they withdrew into the cool mountains.

In summer the mountain hare eats grasses, herbs and leaves. In winter it nibbles twigs, buds and bark of dwarf shrubs and trees. By day it rests well hidden in a shallow hollow, the **form** (in German Sasse), or in a snow cave. It is active mainly at dusk and at night. When in danger it flees in quick zigzags.

The mating season begins in late winter. A female has young two to three times a year, mostly two to four per litter. The young are born with fur and open eyes and quickly become independent. Enemies are the golden eagle, the fox, the eagle owl and the marten.

Because of **global warming**, it is becoming too warm at low altitudes, and the habitat is shrinking upwards. In addition, the brown hare climbs higher and competes with the mountain hare. The two species can even interbreed. Researchers in Switzerland are therefore watching how the populations develop.

begriffe.erklaerung: A colouring that makes an animal almost invisible in its surroundings.
A species that has survived since the ice age in cold refuges.
The shallow hollow in which a hare rests, called Sasse in German.
The shedding of the old coat and the growing of a new one.

gewusst: The rock ptarmigan and the stoat also turn white in winter.
Mountain hares can spread their hind toes wide so that the feet become even broader.

teile.einleitung: Sexual dimorphism means that males and females of the same animal species look clearly different on the outside. The best-known example is the peacock: the male wears a magnificent fan, and the female is plain brown.
wichtigste: Sexual dimorphism means clear outward differences between males and females of the same species.
Differences occur in size, colour, feathers, antlers, horns or mane.
The peacock is a famous example.
Often the male is larger or more colourful, but sometimes it is the female.
One main reason is sexual selection, that is, the choice of mates and competition for mates.
Differences only in colour are called sexual dichromatism.

abschnitte.text: The word **sexual dimorphism** comes from Greek and Latin and means roughly “two forms according to sex”. It is used when you can tell the males and females of a species apart just by looking. In many animals, such as blackbirds, this is easy: the male is black with a yellow beak, and the female brown. In other species, for example many gulls, both sexes look almost the same.

In the peacock, the male carries long, shimmering tail feathers with eyespots, and the female is inconspicuous. In the mallard, too, the drake with its glossy green head is much more colourful than the brown female. A difference only in colour is called **sexual dichromatism**. The plain colour protects the females when they incubate, because they are better camouflaged that way.

In many mammals, the males are larger and stronger. A male gorilla can weigh about twice as much as a female. Red deer carry **antlers**, male ibex have much longer horns than the females, and male lions have a mane. These features help in fights with rivals or impress the females.

There is also the opposite case. In many **spiders**, the females are much larger than the males, for example in the wasp spider. In birds of prey such as the sparrowhawk, too, the female is clearly larger. An extreme example is some deep-sea anglerfishes, in which the tiny male grows fast to the female.

One main reason is **sexual selection**: features that help in courting mates are inherited more often. In addition, males and females often have different tasks, such as incubating or defending a territory. Large females can, for example, form more eggs. In humans too there is a small sexual dimorphism, for example in average body height.

begriffe.erklaerung: Clear outward differences between males and females of a species.
Different colouring of males and females.
An opponent who fights for the same thing, for example for a female.
Colouring or shape that makes an animal hard to spot.

gewusst: In some deep-sea anglerfishes the male is much smaller than the female and lives grown fast to her.
Young male peacocks at first still look like females, and the magnificent fan grows only after some years.
In many birds of prey the female is larger than the male.

teile.einleitung: Pure white cats with blue eyes are strikingly often deaf. The reason lies in their genes: the inherited trait that causes the white fur and the blue eyes often also disturbs development in the inner ear. The naturalist Charles Darwin already described this odd connection.
wichtigste: Pure white cats with blue eyes are deaf more often than other cats.
The gene for white fur and blue eyes is often linked to faulty development of the cochlea.
Depending on the study, about two thirds or more of white cats with two blue eyes are deaf.
If a white cat has only one blue eye, often only the ear on that side is deaf.
The deafness develops in the first weeks of life and cannot be cured.
Deaf cats can still lead a good life, best indoors or in a secured garden.

abschnitte.text: Many pure white cats carry a certain inherited trait that experts call **dominant white**. It prevents the pigment cells, the **melanocytes**, from spreading into the skin and fur. That is why the fur stays white, and often the pigment is also missing from the iris, so that the eyes look blue. Albino cats are something different: they have a different gene defect and usually reddish or very pale eyes.

The body needs pigment cells not only for colour but also in the inner ear. In the **cochlea** they help to make a special fluid that is needed for hearing. If they are missing, the fine **hearing cells** die in the first weeks of life. The kitten is born with apparently normal ears, but soon becomes deaf.

In white cats with two blue eyes the majority are deaf, depending on the study about two thirds or more. If the cat has one blue eye and one of another colour, clearly fewer are affected. Then often only the ear on the side of the blue eye is deaf. White cats without blue eyes can also be deaf, but much more rarely.

A cat that is deaf on one side behaves almost normally, so you often do not notice. Completely deaf cats do not react to calling, clapping or the vacuum cleaner, but they sense vibrations. Vets can measure hearing with a painless **hearing test** that records the brain waves in response to clicking sounds. Responsible breeders test white cats before they carry on breeding with them.

Deaf cats are normal, playful animals and do not suffer from their deafness. Outdoors, however, they are in danger, because they cannot hear cars or dogs. You communicate with them through **hand signals**, light or tapping on the floor. If you do not want to startle a deaf cat, it is best to approach it in such a way that it can see you.

begriffe.erklaerung: A section of the genetic material that controls a certain trait.
A snail-shaped part of the inner ear in which sound is turned into nerve signals.
Cells that make the pigment for skin, hair and eyes.
Unable to hear, or hardly able to hear.

gewusst: As early as 1859, in his famous book on the origin of species, Charles Darwin mentioned that white cats with blue eyes are usually deaf.
A similar connection between white colour and deafness also occurs in dogs such as the Dalmatian.
Many deaf cats miaow especially loudly, because they cannot hear their own voice.

teile.einleitung: Spinnerets are small organs on the abdomen of spiders from which the silk threads come. With them spiders build webs, egg cocoons and safety lines. Spider silk is one of the most astonishing materials in nature.
wichtigste: The spinnerets sit at the end of a spider's abdomen.
Most spiders have six spinnerets in three pairs.
Silk glands open into the spinnerets and make liquid silk.
Only when it is drawn out does the liquid silk become a solid thread.
A spider can make different kinds of thread for different purposes.
In proportion to its weight, spider silk is stronger than steel.
Insects such as the silkworm do not spin their threads with spinnerets, but with glands at the mouth.

abschnitte.text: Spinnerets are small, movable cones on the underside of the **abdomen**. On them sit many tiny spinning tubes from which the silk comes out. Most spiders have three pairs, so six spinnerets. The spider can move them like fingers and so shape the threads.

In the abdomen lie various **silk glands** that make a liquid protein mass. When this is pressed through the spinnerets and drawn out, the proteins rearrange themselves and become solid. The spider mostly pulls the thread out with its hind legs, or sticks it fast and then walks away. Several fine threads can be joined into a thicker thread.

A garden spider can make several kinds of **spider silk**. There are very strong threads for the frame of the web, elastic and sticky capture threads for the spiral, and soft silk for the egg cocoon. Almost every spider trails a safety thread behind it as it walks, on which it can abseil if it falls. Not all spiders build webs, but all can make silk.

Young spiders and small species can travel through the air on silk threads. They climb on to a blade of grass, stretch the abdomen up and let threads out of the spinnerets until the wind carries them off. This **ballooning** is often seen in autumn, when glittering threads float over the meadows. That time is therefore also called Indian summer, or in German Altweibersommer.

Spider silk is very light, elastic and at the same time extremely strong. That is why researchers try to rebuild it artificially, for example for **medicine**, surgical threads or especially light fabrics. Spiders themselves cannot be farmed like silkworms, because they would eat one another. That is why bacteria or yeasts are now made to produce the silk proteins.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gland in the abdomen that makes the liquid silk.
The material of spider threads, a strong protein.
A thread that a spider always trails behind it so as not to fall far if it falls.
A case of silk in which the spider protects its eggs.

gewusst: Some spiders eat their old web in order to reuse the valuable proteins.
A spider's thread is much thinner than a human hair.
Darwin's bark spider from Madagascar builds webs that can be stretched across rivers.

teile.einleitung: A stampede is a wild, panicked flight of a whole herd of animals. When a herd of bison, cattle or wildebeest suddenly runs off in panic, the ground can shake. Weaker animals are often trampled in the process.
wichtigste: A stampede is a mass flight of a herd in panic.
When a herd of bison runs off in panic, it is called a stampede.
The triggers are often predators, thunderstorms, fire or loud noises.
The word comes from the Spanish “estampida” and means roughly a stamping or a bang.
Bison can reach over 50 kilometres per hour when fleeing.
In the Wild West, cowboys feared stampedes of their herds of cattle.
For crowds of people, too, the word stampede is sometimes used, meaning a mass panic.

abschnitte.text: A **stampede** happens when many herd animals take fright at the same time and run blindly in one direction. One animal runs off, the others follow without knowing what they are fleeing from. This behaviour is called the **herd instinct**. In the crowd each single animal is better protected from predators, but in a panic the herd itself can become dangerous.

Typical triggers are predators such as wolves or lions that attack a herd. Thunder, lightning, prairie fires or a sudden bang can also throw animals into a panic. In the past, even the rattle of a pan in the cowboys’ camp was sometimes enough. Herd animals are **prey animals** and would rather react too early than too late to danger.

In the past, huge herds of **American bison** roamed across the prairies of North America. Bison weigh up to a tonne, but can still run faster than 50 kilometres per hour. Some Indigenous peoples deliberately drove herds of bison over cliffs in order to hunt them. A well-known place for this is Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump in Canada, today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In East Africa, over a million **wildebeest** migrate every year together with zebras through the Serengeti and the Masai Mara. When they cross rivers such as the Mara, the animals crowd on to the bank and often plunge into the water in panic. Crocodiles lie in wait there, and in the rush many animals drown or are injured. These river crossings are among the most impressive natural spectacles in the world.

In the 19th century, cowboys drove large **herds of cattle** for hundreds of kilometres to the railway stations. A stampede at night was feared, because animals and riders could be killed or hurt. The cowboys therefore often sang softly to the cattle to calm them. Today the big rodeo festival, the Calgary Stampede in Canada, which has existed since 1912, recalls that time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tendency of herd animals to do what the others do.
An animal that saves itself from danger mainly by running away.
A wide grassland in North America.
When a large crowd becomes afraid and flees out of control.

gewusst: A running herd of bison can be heard and felt as a rumble from a long way off.
Despite their weight, bison are good jumpers and swimmers.
The Calgary Stampede attracts over a million visitors every year.

teile.einleitung: Most fishes are covered with scales that lie on top of one another like roof tiles. They protect the body, for example in the goldfish, and help the fish to glide well through the water. There are quite different kinds of fish scales.
wichtigste: Fish scales are thin bony plates that sit in the skin.
They lie overlapping like roof tiles and leave the fish flexible.
Over the scales lies a layer of slime that protects against germs.
Experts distinguish cycloid scales, ctenoid scales, ganoid scales and placoid scales.
A fish usually keeps the same number of scales, they simply grow with it.
Lost scales can grow back.
Some fishes such as the wels catfish have no scales at all.

abschnitte.text: Fish scales grow in the dermis and consist of **bony material**. They overlap like the **roof tiles** on a house, with the free edges pointing backwards. In this way they protect against knocks, scratches and bites. In the goldfish and many other fishes they cover almost the whole body.

Over the scales lies a thin outer skin that produces **slime**. This slime makes the fish slippery and keeps bacteria, fungi and parasites away. It also reduces resistance in the water. That is why you should touch a fish only with wet hands, so that the protective layer is not damaged.

Carp, trout and whitefish have smooth **cycloid scales**. The perch has **ctenoid scales** with small teeth on the edge, which is why it feels rough. Sturgeons have hard ganoid scales or bony plates. Sharks and rays carry placoid scales, which are built like tiny teeth.

The silvery shine of many fishes is produced by tiny crystals of **guanine** in the skin. The colours of a goldfish come from pigment cells that lie under the transparent scales. Among bred forms of the carp there is the mirror carp with only a few large scales and the leather carp with almost no scales. The wels catfish in Swiss lakes also has a bare, slimy skin.

Along the side of the body in many fishes runs the **lateral line**, a row of scales with small pores. With it the fish senses movements of the water, for example of enemies or prey. Because the scales grow with the fish, rings form from which you can read a fish's age. Experts often also count the scales along the lateral line in order to tell similar species apart.

begriffe.erklaerung: A smooth, round scale such as carp and trout have.
A scale with small teeth on the rear edge, for example in the perch.
A sense organ on the side of the body with which fishes sense water movements.
A substance that produces the silver shine of fishes in small crystals.

gewusst: From fish scales, a pearl essence used to be obtained with which artificial pearls were made shiny.
Shark skin is so rough that it used to be used as sandpaper.

teile.einleitung: The minotaur beetle is a shiny black dung beetle whose male carries three horns on its pronotum. With them it looks like a little armoured bull. It lives mainly in sandy areas and collects droppings from rabbits and sheep.
wichtigste: The minotaur beetle belongs to the dung beetle family.
It is about 1.5 to 2 centimetres long and shiny black.
The male typically carries three horns on its pronotum.
The horns are probably used for fights with other males.
Minotaur beetles and their larvae often feed on the droppings of rabbits and sheep.
It likes best to live on sandy heaths and pastures.
Male and female work together to build the brood tunnel.

abschnitte.text: The minotaur beetle grows to about 14 to 20 millimetres long and is black and shiny. The male has three horns on the **pronotum**. Two long horns point forwards and reach beyond the head, with a short third horn between them. The females have only small bumps. Its scientific name is Typhaeus typhoeus.

The minotaur beetle is found in western and central Europe. It needs loose, **sandy soil** in which it can dig well. Typical places are heaths, dunes, sandy pastures and woodland edges. Many rabbits or sheep often live there, and it needs their droppings.

Minotaur beetles are **dung feeders**. They collect mainly the small, dry droppings of rabbits and sheep. They take these underground, where they are food for the larvae. In this way they help to break down dung and to fertilise the soil.

abschnitte.titel: Caring for the young as a pair
abschnitte.text: Male and female work together, which is rare among beetles. The female digs a vertical **brood tunnel**, which can be over a metre deep. The male carries the soil out and fetches droppings. At the end of the tunnel the droppings are pressed into a sort of dung sausage, on which the female lays an egg. The **larva** eats the store and pupates in the soil.

With his horns the male defends the brood tunnel against other males. When two males fight, they try to push each other out of the tunnel. Bigger males with longer horns usually have better chances. Such **horns** in beetles often have exactly this purpose.

abschnitte.titel: Active in the winter half of the year
abschnitte.text: Unlike many other beetles, the minotaur beetle is active mainly in the cool season. It can be seen from autumn until spring, sometimes even on mild winter days. In summer it rests deep in the soil. Because heaths and pastures with rabbits are becoming rarer, it has become rare in many places.

begriffe.erklaerung: A beetle family whose members feed on the droppings of larger animals.
The armoured part between a beetle’s head and its wing cases.
The young stage of an insect, which still looks quite different from the grown animal.
Everything that parent animals do to look after and protect their offspring.

gewusst: The brood tunnel of a minotaur beetle can reach deeper than a child is tall.
In the minotaur beetle the males help with building the nest, which is only rarely the case in insects.

teile.einleitung: The tiger shark is a large shark from warm seas that has dark stripes like a big cat. It is regarded as one of the least fussy eaters in the sea and eats almost anything it finds. At several metres long, it is one of the largest predatory fish.
wichtigste: The tiger shark has stripes on its skin like a big cat.
Its scientific name is Galeocerdo cuvier.
It belongs to the order of ground sharks (Carcharhiniformes).
The tiger shark is the only living species of its genus.
It eats almost anything it finds.
It lives in tropical and subtropical seas all over the world.
Its snout is short, broad and blunt.

abschnitte.text: The tiger shark gets its name from the dark **cross stripes**, which can be seen best in young animals. In older animals they fade. Its snout is short, broad and blunt. Most adult tiger sharks are three to four metres long, and very large females grow to over five metres long and weigh several hundred kilograms.

Tiger sharks live in tropical and subtropical seas around the world, for example around Hawaii, Australia, in the Caribbean and in the Indian Ocean. They often stay near the coast, in lagoons, river mouths and at coral reefs. At night they often come into shallow water, and by day they tend to swim in deeper water. Some animals cover thousands of kilometres on their migrations.

The tiger shark is not fussy and eats almost anything it finds. Its menu includes fish, other sharks, sea turtles, seabirds, sea snakes, seals and carrion. With its serrated, cockscomb-shaped **teeth** it can even crack turtle shells. In the stomachs of tiger sharks, people have found number plates, plastic and other rubbish.

The tiger shark was first described scientifically in 1822 as **Squalus cuvier**, and it bears its species name in honour of the naturalist Georges Cuvier. The genus Galeocerdo was set up by Johannes Müller and Jakob Henle in 1837. The name is put together from the Greek words for “shark” and “fox”. In the past it was counted among the requiem sharks, but the Catalog of Fishes and FishBase now place it in a family of its own, the **Galeocerdonidae**.

Unlike many other sharks, tiger sharks do not lay eggs in the water. The young develop in eggs inside the mother and hatch there before they are born alive. A litter can consist of 10 to 80 young. The newborns are about half a metre long and are on their own at once.

The tiger shark is one of the few sharks that can also be dangerous to people, and after the great white shark it causes the most bite accidents. Such accidents are very rare, though. The danger coming from people is much greater, because tiger sharks are caught for their fins, meat and liver. The International Union for Conservation of Nature classes the tiger shark as **near threatened**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large order of sharks that also includes hammerhead sharks and catsharks, for example.
The flesh of dead animals.
A group of very closely related species.
Sense organs on the head of sharks with which they detect weak electric fields.

gewusst: With their sense organs, tiger sharks can detect the weak electric signals of animals hidden in the sand.
Because tiger sharks eat so many different things, they are sometimes called the “rubbish bins of the sea”.
A female tiger shark can give birth to as many as 80 young at one time.

teile.einleitung: The mirror test is an experiment with which researchers want to find out whether an animal recognises itself in a mirror. To do this, the animal is given a patch of colour, without noticing, in a place that it can see only in the mirror. If it then examines the patch on its own body, it has probably understood: that is me in the mirror!
wichtigste: The mirror test was developed in 1970 by the American psychologist Gordon Gallup.
It is also called the mark test, because the animal is given a coloured mark.
Chimpanzees, orangutans and other great apes often pass the test.
Some Asian elephants recognise themselves in the mirror, but not all of them.
Bottlenose dolphins and magpies have also passed the test in experiments.
Human children usually pass the test from about the age of one and a half to two.
An animal that does not pass the test is not necessarily stupid, because many animals rely more on smell than on sight.

abschnitte.text: First the animal gets used to a large mirror. Then it is given an odourless **patch of colour** on its forehead or behind its ear, often during anaesthesia or without noticing. Then the researchers watch whether the animal in front of the mirror touches or examines the patch on its own body. If it does, the test counts as passed.

Gordon Gallup carried out the first experiments in 1970 with **chimpanzees**. At first the apes threatened their reflection as if it were a strange animal. After a few days, however, they used the mirror to look at their teeth or their back. Later orangutans and bonobos also passed the test.

abschnitte.titel: Elephants in front of the mirror
abschnitte.text: In 2006 researchers at the Bronx Zoo in New York set up a huge mirror for **Asian elephants**. The elephant cow Happy repeatedly touched a white cross on her head, which she could see only in the mirror, with her trunk. Two other elephants, on the other hand, did not pass the test. So some elephants recognise themselves, but by no means all.

**Bottlenose dolphins**, a species of dolphin, also turned in front of the mirror to look at marks on their bodies. In 2008, experiments in Germany showed that magpies try to rub off a coloured dot on their throat. In 2019 the little cleaner wrasse caused a stir because it tried to rub a mark off on a rock. Whether the fish really recognises itself is disputed among experts.

Many animals rely more on the nose or the ears than on the eyes. Dogs, for example, do not pass the mirror test, but recognise their own **smell** very well. That is why experts say that the test measures only one kind of self-recognition. An animal that fails can still be clever and have a sense of itself.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ability to notice that you yourself are meant, for example in a reflection.
Another name for the mirror test, in which a patch of colour is painted on the body.
Knowing that you are a being of your own, separate from the others.
Science that studies how and why animals behave as they do.

gewusst: Many babies at first take their reflection for another child and smile at it.
The elephant cow Happy from the Bronx Zoo became world famous through the mirror test.
A budgerigar often chirps with its reflection, because it thinks it sees a friend.

teile.einleitung: Social grooming means that animals clean each other's fur. In monkeys such as baboons, this is often called picking lice. It is not only about cleanliness, but above all about friendship and cohesion in the group.
wichtigste: In social grooming, animals clean each other's fur.
In monkeys it is often called picking lice.
Baboons groom each other's fur and so strengthen their bonds.
Grooming removes dirt, flakes of skin and parasites.
It calms the animals and reduces stress.
Horses, cattle, birds and many other animals also groom each other.
Lower ranking animals often groom higher ranking animals.

abschnitte.text: In **social grooming**, one animal cleans the fur or plumage of another animal. Experts also speak of allogrooming, from the English grooming for care. Monkeys part the hair with their fingers, look for dirt, flakes of skin and small **parasites** and remove them with fingers or lips. Because this looks as if they were searching for lice, it is often called **picking lice**.

In baboons and other monkeys, grooming is above all a sign of friendship. It strengthens the **bonds** between the animals of a group. After a quarrel, monkeys often groom each other in order to make up. Animals that groom each other often also help each other in conflicts and are more likely to share food.

When a monkey is groomed, it visibly relaxes and often closes its eyes. In the body, **happiness hormones** are released that calm and reduce stress. That is why the animals gladly accept the grooming. Some species of monkey spend a considerable part of their day grooming each other.

In many groups of monkeys there is a **rank order**. Lower ranking animals often groom higher ranking animals in order to get on well with them. Mothers groom their young especially often. Who grooms whom tells researchers a great deal about the relationships in a group.

It is not only monkeys that groom one another. Horses nibble each other on the withers and the neck, which you can also observe on Swiss pastures. Cows lick each other on the head and neck. Many birds, such as parrots, preen each other's plumage. Bats, meerkats and lions also know this **body care** within the group.

begriffe.erklaerung: Searching and cleaning each other's fur, especially in monkeys.
A living thing that lives on or in another living thing and harms it.
The order of who has more or less say in an animal group.
The raised area between the neck and the back in horses and cattle.

gewusst: A well-known researcher suspects that in humans, language has partly replaced grooming, because with words you can keep in contact with many at the same time.
When picking lice, monkeys mostly find no lice, but above all flakes of skin and dirt.
Horses also have favourite partners when nibbling each other.

teile.einleitung: In sheep shearing, the wool is cut off a sheep. Most domestic sheep do not lose their wool by themselves, so they have to be sheared at least once a year. Afterwards the sheep looks much thinner, because almost all the wool is gone.
wichtigste: Cutting off a sheep's wool is called shearing.
Without shearing, the wool keeps growing and becomes too thick.
Shearing is usually done in spring, so that the sheep does not sweat in summer.
Today an electric shearing machine is mostly used.
After shearing, the sheep has much less wool and looks thinner.
An experienced shearer shears a sheep in a few minutes.
The wool often comes off in one connected piece, the fleece.

abschnitte.text: In **sheep shearing**, the wool is cut off close above the skin. This does not hurt the sheep, rather like having your hair cut. The wool usually comes off as one large, connected piece called a **fleece**. Depending on the breed, a sheep yields about 2 to 6 kilograms of wool.

abschnitte.titel: Why do you have to shear?
abschnitte.text: Wild sheep change their coat by themselves, but most domestic sheep do not, and their wool keeps growing. An unshorn sheep eventually has far too much wool, which becomes heavy and dirty. It suffers from **heat** in summer, and in the matted wool flies can lay their eggs. That is why regular shearing is important for the animal's wellbeing.

In the past, the wool was cut off with large **hand shears**. Today shearers mostly use an electric **shearing machine**. The shearer sits the sheep on its rump and holds it with his legs, so it stays calm. He shears in fixed strokes from the belly over the sides to the back.

In Switzerland, shearing is usually done in spring, before the sheep go out to pasture or up to the Alp. Some breeds are sheared twice a year. Professional shearers travel from farm to farm in the season. There are also competitions in which shearers show how fast and cleanly they work.

The wool is sorted, washed and spun into **yarn** or made into felt. Fine wool is made into jumpers and socks, and coarse wool into carpets or insulation for houses. In Switzerland, sheep's wool brings in little money today. Part of it is therefore also used as fertiliser in the garden.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sheep's whole, connected woolly coat after shearing.
An electric device for cutting off wool.
A person who shears sheep.
A long thread spun from fibres.

gewusst: The Australian sheep Chris carried over 40 kilograms of unshorn wool around with him in 2015.
Top shearers manage several hundred sheep in a day.

teile.einleitung: Turtles and tortoises are reptiles with a hard shell, into which many species can withdraw when in danger. They have existed for over 200 million years, so even longer than many dinosaurs. Some live on land, others in fresh water or in the sea.
wichtigste: Turtles and tortoises are reptiles and belong to the oldest animal groups on Earth.
Their shell consists of bony plates covered with horny scutes.
The upper shell is called the carapace and the lower shell the plastron.
They have no teeth, but a sharp horny beak.
They breathe with lungs, even the water turtles.
There are tortoises, pond and freshwater turtles, and sea turtles.
In Switzerland only the European pond turtle lives in the wild.

abschnitte.text: The shell is the most important feature of turtles and tortoises. It consists of **bony plates** that are fused with the ribs and the backbone, and it is covered on the outside with horny scutes. The domed upper shell is called the **carapace** and the flat lower shell the **plastron**. A turtle therefore cannot slip out of its shell. Many species draw the head and legs in when in danger.

Worldwide there are about 350 species of turtles and tortoises. Tortoises have a highly domed shell and pillar-like legs. Pond and freshwater turtles have a flatter shell and webbing between the toes. Sea turtles such as the green turtle have flippers instead of feet. The largest tortoises live on the **Galápagos Islands** and the Seychelles and can weigh over 200 kilograms.

Turtles and tortoises have no teeth, but cut up their food with a sharp **horny beak**. Tortoises eat mainly herbs, leaves and flowers. The pond turtle eats worms, snails, insect larvae, tadpoles and small fishes. Some sea turtles eat jellyfish or seagrass.

All turtles breathe with lungs. Water turtles therefore have to come up to the surface to take in air. Turtles lay eggs, which they place on land in a pit they have dug themselves. In many species the **temperature** in the nest decides whether males or females hatch from the eggs. The parents do not look after the young.

Turtles and tortoises can get very old. Large tortoises often reach over 100 years. Because they move slowly and have a low metabolism, they need little energy. Many tortoises from colder regions go into **hibernation** in winter.

Many species of turtles and tortoises are threatened, for example by loss of habitat, poaching and plastic in the sea. In Switzerland lives the **European pond turtle**, which is very rare and protected. In the canton of Geneva and in other places there are projects to resettle it. Released pets such as American red-eared sliders compete with the native animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: The upper shell of the turtle.
The lower shell of the turtle.
A cold-blooded vertebrate with scales or horny scutes, for example a lizard, snake or turtle.
A resting state in winter in which the body almost stands still.

gewusst: The leatherback turtle is the largest turtle in the world and can grow over two metres long.
Sea turtles often return to lay eggs on the beach where they hatched themselves.

teile.einleitung: The anguid lizards, in German Schleichen, are a family of lizards that includes the slow worm. Many of them have no legs and therefore look like snakes. They are not snakes, however, but close relatives of the lizards.
wichtigste: Anguid lizards are a family of lizards and not snakes.
The best known example in Europe and Switzerland is the slow worm.
Many anguid lizards have no legs or only tiny ones.
Unlike snakes, they have movable eyelids.
When in danger, many anguid lizards can shed their tail.
They eat mainly snails, worms and insects.
Anguid lizards live in Europe, Asia and America.

abschnitte.text: The anguid lizards form a family within the **lizards**, to which over 100 species belong worldwide. They include legless species such as the slow worm and the European legless lizard, but also species with short legs such as the American alligator lizards. The German name comes from the fact that many of them move slowly, in a creeping way. Because of their missing legs they are often taken for snakes.

Anguid lizards have **eyelids** and can blink, which snakes cannot. Their body is covered with smooth, shiny scales, under which lie small bony plates. Their tongue is only slightly notched and not as deeply forked as in snakes. Many anguid lizards can shed their tail, which is called **autotomy**. In the skeleton you also still find remains of shoulder and pelvis bones.

The **slow worm** is the only anguid lizard in Switzerland and one of the most common reptiles in the country. It usually grows to about 30 to 45 centimetres long and is brownish, grey or copper coloured. Despite its German name, which means blind creeper, it is not blind, and it has small, well working eyes. You find it in gardens, at the edges of forests, in meadows and hedges, right up into the mountains.

Anguid lizards are hunters that mainly eat slow prey. The slow worm especially likes to eat **slugs** and earthworms. In addition there are spiders, woodlice and insect larvae. That is why it is very welcome to gardeners.

Anguid lizards are shy and like to hide under stones, boards or leaves. The slow worm spends the winter in **hibernation** in the ground, often together with other animals. The slow worm gives birth to live young, mostly in late summer. The young are only about 7 to 10 centimetres long and shine silvery with a dark back.

Slow worms are often killed by cats, lawnmowers and cars. Some people kill them because they take them for snakes. In Switzerland all reptiles, and so the slow worm too, are **protected**. Natural gardens with piles of stones, leaves and hedges help them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reptile, mostly with legs, for example a wall lizard or a gecko.
The shedding of the tail in order to escape an enemy.
A fold of skin with which an animal can close its eye.
The legless lizard that also lives in Switzerland.

gewusst: In captivity, slow worms can live for over 40 years.
The European legless lizard from south-eastern Europe is the largest anguid lizard in Europe and grows over a metre long.

teile.einleitung: The walk is the slowest gait of the horse. The horse puts its four hooves down one after another, quite calmly and evenly. For riders, the walk is the first gait they learn.
wichtigste: The walk is the slowest of the three basic gaits: walk, trot and canter.
At a walk, a horse moves about as fast as a person walking briskly.
It is a four-beat gait, because you hear four separate hoofbeats.
At a walk, two or three hooves are always on the ground at the same time.
Unlike trot and canter, there is no moment of suspension.
On the pasture, horses walk almost all day while they graze.

abschnitte.text: The **walk** is one of the three **basic gaits** that all horses have. The other two are the trot and the canter. The walk is the calmest and most energy-saving way of moving. At a walk, a horse covers about 6 to 7 kilometres an hour.

At a walk, the horse puts its legs down in a fixed order, for example hind left, front left, hind right, front right. This is called a **four-beat gait**, because four even beats are heard. In this, at least two hooves are always on the ground. That is why the **moment of suspension**, in which no hoof touches the ground, is missing.

At a walk, the horse nods its head and neck in time with the movement. This **nodding movement** helps it to keep its balance. The back swings gently to and fro, which feels like rocking to the rider. That is why the walk is especially pleasant for beginners.

Every riding lesson usually begins and ends with walk, so that the muscles warm up and relax again. In **dressage**, people distinguish different kinds, such as the collected walk, the medium walk and the extended walk. In a walk on a **long rein**, the horse may stretch its neck and loosen up. A good, active walk with an even rhythm is regarded as a sign of a healthy horse.

Some breeds have additional gaits, for example the **Icelandic horse** with the tölt and the pace. The tölt is also a four-beat gait, but much faster than the walk. In Switzerland you often see Franches-Montagnes horses at a walk, ridden on hiking trails or harnessed to carriages. On long trail rides lasting many hours, too, horses go mainly at a walk, because it costs little energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The way a horse moves its legs, for example walk, trot or canter.
You hear four separate hoofbeats one after another.
A short moment in which no hoof touches the ground.
The reins are left loose so that the horse can stretch.

gewusst: A horse can be on the move at a walk for many hours without getting tired.
Experts can sometimes tell from an uneven walk that a horse is lame.

teile.einleitung: House centipedes are centipedes with astonishingly long legs that dart across walls and floors in a flash. The best-known species, Scutigera coleoptrata, often lives in houses, cellars and bathrooms. Many people are frightened at the sight of them, yet these animals are useful insect hunters.
wichtigste: House centipedes belong to the centipedes and not to the spiders or insects.
The commonest species in Europe is called Scutigera coleoptrata.
Adult animals have 15 pairs of legs, which get longer and longer towards the back.
The body is only about two to three centimetres long, but with the legs they look much bigger.
House centipedes hunt insects, silverfish and small spiders at night.
They are harmless to people.
They originally come from the Mediterranean region.

abschnitte.text: The house centipede has a yellowish grey body with dark stripes along its length. Its 15 pairs of legs are long and thin, and the hindmost are the longest. On its head it carries very long **antennae**, with which it feels and smells. Unlike many centipedes, it has large eyes made up of many single eyes and can see well.

Originally Scutigera coleoptrata lives in the warm **Mediterranean region** under stones and in rock crevices. With people it has spread widely and today also lives in central Europe and North America. In Switzerland you find it mainly in buildings, for example in cellars, bathrooms and old houses, and in warm areas such as Ticino also outdoors. It likes it damp and dark.

House centipedes are among the fastest creepy-crawlies and manage about 40 centimetres per second. At night they hunt flies, silverfish, cockroaches, moths and small spiders. They seize the prey with the **venom claws**, a modified first pair of legs, and paralyse it with venom. Sometimes they hold several prey animals at the same time with their legs.

If a house centipede is grabbed by a leg, it can simply drop it and flee. This dropping of body parts is called **autotomy**. At the next moults the leg grows back. Young house centipedes, by the way, hatch with only four pairs of legs and get more with every moult.

The house centipede is not dangerous to people. Its venom claws are so small that they hardly penetrate human skin, and even then it feels at most like a mosquito bite. Because it eats **pests** such as silverfish and cockroaches, it is actually a helper in the house. If you do not like it, you can take it outside with a glass and a sheet of paper.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of arthropods with many pairs of legs and venom claws.
A modified foremost pair of legs with which centipedes inject venom into prey.
An animal itself drops a body part when in danger.
Shedding the old body covering that has become too small.

gewusst: Despite the name, no centipede has exactly 100 legs, and the house centipede has 30.
The hindmost legs of the house centipede can be longer than its whole body.
House centipedes carefully clean their legs and antennae with their mouthparts after eating.

teile.einleitung: Ichneumon wasps, in German Schlupfwespen, are insects that lay their eggs in or on other insects, for example in aphids or caterpillars. The larvae then eat their host from the inside. That sounds gruesome, but it makes ichneumon wasps important helpers against pests.
wichtigste: Ichneumon wasps are hymenopterans and are related to bees, ants and wasps.
They lay their eggs in or on other insects or spiders.
Their larvae develop in the host and finally kill it.
Some ichneumon wasps lay their eggs in aphids and are their natural enemies.
They do not sting people.
In gardens and greenhouses they are used for pest control.
There are tens of thousands of species, and many are tiny.

abschnitte.text: Ichneumon wasps are a very large group of **hymenopterans**. Worldwide, tens of thousands of species are known, and many have not yet been described at all. Some are only a millimetre small, others several centimetres. Many females have a long **ovipositor** on the abdomen that looks like a sting. They do not sting people with it, however, but lay eggs.

A female ichneumon wasp searches with her antennae for a suitable **host**, such as a caterpillar, a beetle larva or an aphid. With the ovipositor she lays one or more eggs in or on the host. The hatched larva slowly eats the host from the inside. An animal that lives in this way is called a **parasitoid**, because it kills its host in the end. Then the larva pupates, and a new ichneumon wasp hatches.

Some small ichneumon wasps lay one egg each in an aphid. The aphid dies and becomes a hard, swollen shell that is called an **aphid mummy**. Later the young wasp hatches from a small round hole. Together with ladybirds and lacewings, ichneumon wasps are among the most important natural enemies of aphids.

Because they kill pests, ichneumon wasps are regarded as **beneficial insects**. In greenhouses they are used on purpose, for example against the whitefly on tomatoes. Tiny ichneumon wasps of the genus Trichogramma help in maize fields against the European corn borer, a moth. In households, certain species help against clothes moths. In this way less poison is needed, and that is good for the environment.

In Switzerland too, thousands of species of ichneumon wasps live. You find them in gardens, meadows and forests, often on flowers, where they drink nectar. Swiss farmers use ichneumon wasps in **biological pest control**. Flowering meadows and hedges help to ensure that enough ichneumon wasps occur.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that grows up in a host and kills it in doing so.
A tube on the abdomen with which the female lays eggs.
An animal that helps people, for example against pests.
The empty, hard shell of an aphid in which an ichneumon wasp has developed.

gewusst: Some giant ichneumon wasps can drill several centimetres deep into wood with their ovipositor to reach a beetle larva.
Among the parasitic wasps in the wider sense are some of the smallest insects in the world, smaller than a grain of dust.

teile.einleitung: The death's-head hawkmoth is a large night-flying moth with a yellow marking on its back that looks like a skull. It is the largest hawkmoth in Europe and flies as a migrant from Africa and southern Europe as far as Switzerland. It can also squeak and steals honey from beehives.
wichtigste: The death's-head hawkmoth belongs to the hawkmoth family (Sphingidae).
Its scientific name is Acherontia atropos.
Carl Linnaeus first described it in 1758, at that time under the genus name Sphinx.
It has a skull-like yellow marking on the thorax.
It is the largest hawkmoth in Europe.
Females reach a wingspan of about 10 to 12 cm.
It is a migrant moth that flies to us from the south.

abschnitte.text: On its thorax the moth has a yellow marking that reminds people of a **skull**. The forewings are marbled dark brown, and the hind wings are ochre yellow with two dark bands. Females reach a wingspan of about 10 to 12 centimetres, rarely up to 13 centimetres, and weigh about 3 to 8 grams. The antennae are black with a white tip.

Carl Linnaeus described the moth in 1758 and at first placed it in the genus **Sphinx**. The present genus name Acherontia goes back to the Acheron, a river of the Greek underworld. The species name recalls **Atropos**, one of the three Fates of Greek legend, who cuts the thread of life. Because of its appearance, the moth was once regarded as a bringer of bad luck.

The death's-head hawkmoth lives mainly in Africa and around the Mediterranean. In early summer some moths fly as **migrants** over the Alps to central Europe and Switzerland. Here they lay eggs, from which a new generation hatches in late summer. The pupae usually do not survive the cold winter here.

The caterpillar feeds mainly on potatoes, tomatoes and other **nightshades**. It grows to about 12 centimetres long and is mostly yellow-green with blue slanting stripes. At the rear end it has a curved horn, like many hawkmoth caterpillars. To turn into a pupa it digs deep into the soil.

The death's-head hawkmoth has a short, strong proboscis and breaks into **beehives** at night to drink honey. It smells similar to the bees and is therefore often not attacked. If it is disturbed, it can make a high squeak by pressing air through its proboscis. The caterpillar and the pupa can also make sounds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of strong, fast-flying night moths.
A butterfly or moth that flies over long distances to other regions every year.
The three goddesses of destiny in Greek legend.
A plant family that includes the potato, tomato and pepper.

gewusst: The death's-head hawkmoth is one of the few butterflies and moths that can make audible sounds.
There are three species of death's-head hawkmoth worldwide, called Acherontia atropos, Acherontia lachesis and Acherontia styx.
In the past people were afraid of the moth, because they took the skull on its back for an evil sign.

teile.einleitung: Purring is the deep, even rumble that cats make as they breathe in and out. Mostly they purr when they feel comfortable, but sometimes also when they are afraid or in pain. Researchers even suspect that purring might help with healing.
wichtigste: Purring is a deep rumble of cats as they breathe in and out.
It is produced by fast movements of the muscles in the larynx.
The frequency is roughly between 25 and 150 vibrations per second.
Cats purr when they are content, but also when stressed or in pain.
Even young kittens purr when suckling from their mother.
Domestic cats and many small cats purr, lions and tigers do not.
It is suspected that the vibration could promote the healing of bones and tissue.

abschnitte.text: Purring is an even, vibrating rumble that cats make with the mouth closed. Unlike in miaowing, it goes on as they **breathe in** and as they **breathe out**. Often you can not only hear it but feel it if you put your hand on the cat. A cat can purr for hours.

Purring is produced in the **larynx**. Muscles there contract and relax again very fast, so that the glottis becomes narrow and wide in quick rhythm. As a result, the air begins to vibrate. The frequency is roughly between 25 and 150 **hertz**, that is, vibrations per second. More recent research shows that special pads on the vocal folds play a role in this.

Most often cats purr when they are relaxed, are being stroked or are snuggling up to someone. Young kittens purr a few days after birth when suckling, and the mother purrs back. In this way they show that everything is all right. But cats also purr when they are ill, injured or stressed. Then the purring probably serves to **calm** themselves.

Some researchers suspect that purring might have a **healing-promoting** effect. Vibrations in the range of about 25 to 50 hertz are being studied in medicine, because they might stimulate the growth of bone. That would explain why cats also purr when they are injured. However, it has not yet been proved for certain. Many people also simply find purring soothing.

Besides domestic cats, many other small cats such as the lynx, the puma and the **cheetah** purr. Big cats such as the lion, the tiger and the leopard, by contrast, can roar, but cannot purr continuously. Their larynx is built differently. A few other animals also make similar rumbling sounds, but true purring is typical of cats.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organ in the throat in which sounds and tones are produced.
A unit that measures how often something vibrates per second.
A fast swinging back and forth that you can feel.
The gap between the vocal folds in the larynx.

gewusst: Some cats mix a high, demanding tone into their purring when begging for food, which people can hardly ignore.
The cheetah is among the largest cats that can really purr.

teile.einleitung: Gestation is the name for the time in which a female mammal carries young in her body. In humans we call this pregnancy. How long it lasts differs very much from one animal species to another, from just under two weeks to almost two years.
wichtigste: Gestation is the time from fertilisation to birth in animals.
The gestation of a female dog lasts about 63 days.
Large animals usually carry their young longer than small ones.
Elephants carry their young for almost two years.
Cows carry their calf for about nine months.
In the roe deer there is a delay before the embryo develops, which lengthens the gestation.
Vets can detect a pregnancy with ultrasound.
